CHAPTER SUMMARY:

Chapter 12: Beyond Earth

The chapter opens with a narrative of two children in Nubra, Ladakh, who observe the night sky and experience a sense of wonder about stars, setting the context for exploring objects beyond Earth.

12.1 Stars and Constellations

Stars shine with their own light; some are bright and others dim. Groups of stars that appear to form recognisable patterns are called constellations — a term that in modern usage refers to defined regions of the sky rather than just the star patterns themselves. These patterns were historically used for navigation by sailors and travellers before modern technology. The International Astronomical Union (IAU) officially listed 88 constellations in the early twentieth century, dividing the entire sky into 88 regions. Notable constellations include Orion (depicted as a hunter with a three-star belt), Canis Major (which contains Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky), and Taurus. In Indian astronomy, the term nakshatra denotes specific stars or star groups — Betelgeuse in Orion is known as Ardra, the Pleiades cluster in Taurus as Krittika, and Aldebaran in Taurus as Rohini. Two widely known star patterns are the Big Dipper (in constellation Ursa Major, known in India as Saptarishi) and the Little Dipper (in Ursa Minor), which includes the Pole Star (Polaris, or Dhruva tara). The Pole Star appears nearly stationary in the North direction and is used to locate north in the Northern hemisphere. There is a student activity (Activity 12.1) in which students draw imaginary lines between stars to form their own patterns and invent stories about them.

12.2 Night Sky Watching

The visibility of stars depends on light pollution, smoke, dust, and obstructions such as tall buildings and trees; the night sky is best observed from open, dark locations away from city lights. Light pollution — excessive artificial light at night — reduces the number of stars visible and is a growing global concern; dark sky reserves and parks have been established to preserve dark skies for research. Not all stars and constellations are visible from all locations or at all times of the year; the Pole Star, for example, is not visible from the Southern Hemisphere. Sky mapping apps such as Sky Map and Stellarium help identify stars, constellations, and planets from any given location. The section provides practical preparation guidance for night sky watching: choosing a clear moonless night, waiting about half an hour for eyes to adjust to the dark, and using a compass and printed constellation images. Activities 12.2 and 12.3 are student activities in which learners attempt to locate the Big Dipper, the Pole Star, and the constellation Orion with the star Sirius in the actual night sky.

12.3 Our Solar System

The Sun

The Sun is the star closest to Earth — an extremely hot, spherical ball of gases that produces heat and light, making it the primary source of energy on Earth. Its distance from Earth is about 150 million km, defined as one astronomical unit (au), the standard unit for distances within the solar system. The Sun is about 100 times larger than Earth in diameter; it appears large due to its relative proximity, while far more distant stars appear only as points of light. The Sun regulates climate, seasons, weather, the water cycle, and winds, and is essential for plant growth and all life on Earth.

Planets

A planet is a large, nearly spherical object that revolves around the Sun; this movement is called revolution. The eight planets in order of increasing distance from the Sun are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. The inner four planets are smaller and have solid rocky surfaces; the outer four are much larger, mostly made of gas and ice, and have ring-like structures of dust and rocky material around them. The presence of an atmosphere affects a planet's temperature — Venus is hotter than Mercury despite being farther from the Sun because its thick atmosphere traps heat. Venus is known as the Morning Star or Evening Star; Mars is the Red Planet due to its reddish soil; Earth appears blue from space and is called the Blue Planet. Objects reclassified as dwarf planets — including Pluto — were redefined by the IAU in 2006 when similar small objects were discovered beyond Neptune. Activity 12.4 guides students to locate Venus at dawn (eastern horizon before sunrise) or dusk (western horizon after sunset).

Natural Satellites

Objects that move around planets are commonly called satellites; moons are the natural satellites of planets. Earth has one Moon, Mars has two moons, and Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune have large numbers of moons.

The Moon

Earth's natural satellite, the Moon, is about 3,84,000 km away and takes approximately 27 days to complete one revolution around the Earth. The Moon is about a quarter the size of Earth in diameter and has virtually no atmosphere. Its surface features circular bowl-like structures called craters, formed by the impact of asteroids and rocks from space; without atmosphere, water, or life, these features persist for very long periods. India launched Chandrayaan-1 (2008), Chandrayaan-2 (2019), and Chandrayaan-3 (July 2023); the Vikram lander of Chandrayaan-3 successfully soft-landed near the Moon's south pole on 23 August 2023, making India the first country to achieve this, and 23 August is now celebrated as National Space Day.

Asteroids

Asteroids are small, rocky, irregularly shaped objects that revolve around the Sun; many orbit in the region between Mars and Jupiter called the asteroid belt. Their sizes range from about 10 m to approximately 500 km.

Comets

Comets are objects from the outer Solar System composed of dust, gases, rocks, and ice; as they approach the Sun, frozen material evaporates to form a visible tail, but they appear dim as they move away. Many comets orbit the Sun periodically — Halley's Comet, for example, appears every 76 years and was last seen in 1986. The Solar System as a whole consists of the Sun, eight planets, their moons, and many smaller objects including asteroids and comets; all objects other than the Sun shine by reflecting sunlight.

12.4 The Milky Way Galaxy

The Milky Way Galaxy (Akasha Ganga) is visible from very dark locations as a faint extended band of light stretching across the night sky. A galaxy contains millions to billions of stars; our entire Solar System is a small part of the Milky Way Galaxy.

12.5 The Universe

Beyond the Milky Way, there are many other galaxies in outer space that scientists study to understand stars, galaxies, and the Universe as a whole. The search for life elsewhere in the Universe is ongoing and directed mainly toward exoplanets — planets discovered orbiting stars other than our Sun — but no evidence of life has been found yet.

content.text:
CHAPTER SUMMARY:

Chapter 2 — Exploring Substances: Acidic, Basic, and Neutral introduces students to the classification of everyday substances based on their chemical nature, using a National Science Day science fair narrative involving two siblings, Ashwin and Keerthi, as the motivating context. The chapter establishes that substances around us can be sorted into three groups — acidic, basic, and neutral — and that certain natural materials can be used to identify which group a substance belongs to. The chapter is organised around hands-on exploration of three natural indicators and the phenomenon of neutralisation.

2.1 Nature — Our Science Laboratory frames nature as the primary source of tools for scientific investigation. It establishes the concept of an indicator as a substance that shows different colours in the presence of acids and bases, and introduces the term acid-base indicator. This section is organised into three subsections, each focused on a different natural indicator.

2.1.1 Litmus as an indicator explains that litmus is a natural dye obtained from lichens and is available as a solution and as paper strips in two colours — blue and red. The key concepts are that acidic substances turn blue litmus paper red, while basic substances turn red litmus paper blue, and neutral substances cause no colour change in either paper. A Holistic Lens feature notes that lichens are symbiotic associations of a fungus and an alga, found in areas with clean air. The section contains a student activity. Activity 2.1 directs students to test a range of household samples — lemon juice, soap solution, amla juice, tamarind water, vinegar, baking soda solution, lime water, tap water, washing powder solution, sugar solution, and salt solution — with both blue and red litmus papers and sort them into acidic (Group A), basic (Group B), and neutral (Group C) groups. Activity 2.2 asks students to relate taste to acid content, establishing that sour-tasting substances tend to be acidic, and to observe that basic substances are generally soapy or slippery to touch and taste bitter. It introduces citric acid, tartaric acid, ascorbic acid (Vitamin C), and oxalic acid as examples of naturally occurring acids in foods.

2.1.2 Red rose as an indicator extends the concept of natural indicators by showing that an extract prepared from red rose petals can also serve as an acid-base indicator, giving a red colour in acidic solutions and a green colour in basic solutions. Other plant materials mentioned as potential indicators include beetroot, purple cabbage, turmeric, jamun, and red hibiscus (gudhal). A Fascinating Facts box describes how the hydrangea plant produces flowers of different colours depending on whether the soil is acidic or basic. The section contains student activities. Activity 2.3 guides students to prepare a red rose petal extract by crushing petals and filtering the coloured liquid. Activity 2.4 has students test the same set of samples using the red rose extract and compare results with the litmus paper groupings from Activity 2.1.

2.1.3 Turmeric as an indicator demonstrates that turmeric (haldi) paper, prepared by soaking filter paper in turmeric paste and drying it, can be used to detect basic substances. Basic solutions turn turmeric paper from yellow to red, but the paper cannot distinguish between acidic and neutral substances, which both leave it unchanged. A Fascinating Facts box describes turmeric's traditional significance as a member of the ginger family and its use in Ayurvedic medicine. The section contains student activities. Activity 2.5 guides students to prepare turmeric paper strips. Activity 2.6 introduces olfactory indicators — substances whose odour changes in the presence of an acid or a base — and uses onion-soaked strips to investigate this phenomenon. A Know a Scientist feature introduces Acharya Prafulla Chandra Ray, known as the Father of Modern Indian Chemistry, who established India's first pharmaceutical company and advanced scientific research.

2.2 What Happens When Acidic Substances Mix with Basic Substances? introduces the neutralisation reaction through an experiment in which lemon juice (acidic) is progressively neutralised by lime water (basic), observed through the colour change of blue litmus solution. The section establishes that when an acid and a base react in sufficient quantities, the resulting solution is neither acidic nor basic. This type of reaction is defined as a neutralisation reaction, and its products are identified as salt, water, and heat, expressed as: Acid + Base → Salt + Water + Heat. The section contains a student activity.

2.3 Neutralisation in Daily Life applies the concept of neutralisation to three real-world scenarios. Situation 1 explains that a red ant bite injects formic acid into the skin, and applying baking soda (a base) neutralises the acid and relieves the pain. Situation 2 addresses soil that has become too acidic due to excessive use of chemical fertilisers, which can be corrected by adding lime; if soil is too basic, organic matter like compost is added to release acids that neutralise the base. Situation 3 describes how acidic factory waste released into a lake can harm fish, and explains that adding basic substances before release can neutralise the waste. The chapter concludes by revisiting the opening science fair mystery, suggesting that turmeric solution was used to coat the paper and a soap solution was used for writing, so the basic soap turned the turmeric paper red to reveal the message.

CHAPTER SUMMARY:

Chapter 3 — Electricity: Circuits and their Components uses a school trip to the Bhakra Nangal Dam hydroelectric powerhouse as its opening context, framing the broad pervasiveness of electricity in daily life across categories such as cooking, lighting, transportation, heating and cooling, entertainment, and communication. The chapter focuses on the components of a simple electric circuit — electric cell, battery, electric lamp, LED, switch, and wires — and progresses from exploring a familiar object (a torchlight) to understanding how its components work together, how circuits are drawn using symbols, and which materials allow current to flow.

3.1 A Torchlight introduces the torchlight (also called a torch or flashlight) as the entry point for studying electricity. The section uses the familiar observation that the torch lamp glows when the switch is in one position and not the other, prompting students to open the torch and examine what is inside. The section contains a student activity. Activity 3.1 asks students to take a torchlight, observe it carefully for its lamp and switch, slide the switch and observe whether the lamp glows, and then open the torch to find the electric cells inside.

3.2 A Simple Electrical Circuit introduces the internal components of the torch and explains how they function together to form a circuit. It is divided into six subsections.

3.2.1 Electric cell establishes that an electric cell is a portable source of electrical energy with two terminals — a positive terminal (the metal cap, marked +) and a negative terminal (the metal disc, marked –). The section contains a student activity. Activity 3.2 asks students to examine an electric cell carefully and identify its two terminals and their physical features.

3.2.2 Battery explains that when two or more cells are connected so that the positive terminal of one cell connects to the negative terminal of the next, the combination is called a battery. Connecting cells in this way provides electrical energy to the circuit for a longer time or at greater capacity. A Fascinating Facts box notes that the term "battery" is also commonly used for a single cell. The section contains a student activity. Activity 3.3 asks students to take a two-cell torch, remove the cells, reinsert them in different orders and orientations, and observe which arrangement makes the lamp glow, leading to the discovery of the correct series arrangement.

3.2.3 Electric lamp covers two types of lamps. The Incandescent Lamp subsection explains that inside the glass bulb of an incandescent lamp is a thin wire called a filament, which gets hot and glows when current passes through it. The filament is supported by two thicker wires connected to the lamp's two terminals — the metal case and the metal tip. The LED Lamp subsection explains that a Light Emitting Diode (LED) does not contain a filament, has two terminals identified by wire length (the longer wire is positive, the shorter is negative), and can emit light in different colours. Both subsections contain student activities.

3.2.4 Making an electric lamp glow using an electric cell or battery presents the core construction activity of the chapter, where students assemble a circuit using a cell, lamp, cell holder, lamp holder, and wires. The key learning is that a lamp glows only in specific arrangements, prompting comparison between glowing and non-glowing configurations. A separate experiment with an LED highlights that, unlike incandescent lamps, LEDs allow current to flow in one direction only, so the polarity of connections must be correct for the LED to glow. The section contains student activities.

3.2.5 An electrical circuit defines an electrical circuit as a complete path for electric current to flow. The section explains that the direction of current in a circuit is taken to be from the positive to the negative terminal of the electric cell. Current passes through the filament of an incandescent lamp and causes it to glow; the lamp will glow as long as the circuit is complete. A Fascinating Facts box notes that a lamp with a broken filament has "fused" and stops current flow.

3.2.6 Electric switch introduces the switch as a device that either completes (closes) or breaks (opens) a circuit. When the circuit is closed, current flows and the lamp glows (ON position); when the circuit is open, there is a gap and current cannot flow (OFF position). The section guides students to construct a simple switch using drawing pins and a safety pin, and then test it in a circuit. The section contains student activities.

3.3 Circuit Diagrams introduces the use of standard symbols to represent electrical components — electric cell, battery, electric lamp, LED, switch in ON and OFF positions, and wire — so that circuits can be drawn and understood universally. A representation of a circuit using these symbols is called a circuit diagram. The long line in the cell symbol represents the positive terminal, the short line the negative terminal; in the LED symbol, the triangle indicates the direction of current flow and two arrows indicate light emission. International bodies such as the IEC, ANSI, and IEEE establish these standard symbols. The section contains a student activity. Activity 3.10 asks students to draw circuit diagrams for two given circuits — one with an incandescent lamp and one with an LED.

3.4 Electrical Conductors and Insulators investigates why metal wires are used in circuits and why they are covered with plastic or rubber. The section introduces the concept that some materials allow electric current to pass through them easily (good conductors or conductors of electricity) while others do not allow current to pass (insulators or poor conductors of electricity). Experiments show that metals are conductors; plastic, rubber, glass, wood, paper, and wax are insulators. Conductors are used for wires, switches, and connectors, while insulators are used as coverings to protect people from electric shocks. A Dive Deeper box distinguishes Direct Current (DC) from batteries from Alternating Current (AC) from power plants. A safety caution notes that the human body is a conductor and electric current can cause severe injury or death. The section contains a student activity. Activity 3.11 guides students to build a conduction tester and use it to test various objects, recording results in a table and concluding which materials are conductors and which are insulators.

CHAPTER SUMMARY:

Chapter 4 — The World of Metals and Non-metals opens with two students, Yashwant and Anandi, visiting an ironsmith (Sudarshan) in a village in Rajasthan who crafts daily-use items such as tawas, baltis, chimtas, phawras, kulhadis, khurpis, and jelees from iron. Observing that iron can be beaten into shapes motivates the chapter's core inquiry into what properties make metals and non-metals distinct, how they behave with air and water, and what roles they play in daily life.

4.1 Properties of Materials introduces the physical properties used to distinguish metals from non-metals, organised across five subsections.

4.1.1 Malleability establishes that metals such as copper, aluminium, and iron are lustrous (showing metallic lustre) and hard, whereas materials like coal, sulfur, and wood are non-lustrous and not as hard. The property by which materials can be beaten into thin sheets is called malleability, and most metals possess it; gold and silver are identified as the most malleable metals. Materials that break into pieces rather than flatten are called brittle — coal and sulfur are brittle. A Holistic Lens feature connects the prominence of iron in ancient Indian civilisation to the superior strength of iron agricultural tools, noting that copper was likely discovered earlier. The section contains a student activity. Activity 4.1 directs students to collect pieces of copper, aluminium, iron, coal, sulfur, and wood, observe their lustre and hardness, and then hammer each piece to determine whether it flattens or breaks.

4.1.2 Ductility introduces the property by which materials can be drawn into wires as ductility, noting that this property is mainly possessed by metals. Copper and aluminium wires are common in electrical fittings and musical instruments; gold is so ductile that one gram can be drawn into a two-kilometre-long wire. A Dive Deeper box explains that steel ropes — a mixture of iron and carbon — are used in suspension bridges and cranes because of their ability to support heavy loads.

4.1.3 Sonority defines sonority as the property by which metals produce a ringing sound when struck or dropped, as opposed to the dull sounds produced by coal and wood. Metals are described as sonorous in nature; everyday examples include a school bell and the ghungroos worn by dancers. The section contains a student activity. Activity 4.2 asks students to drop a metal spoon, a coin, a piece of coal, and a block of wood and compare the sounds produced.

4.1.4 Conduction of heat establishes through a comparative experiment that metals are good conductors of heat while wood is a poor conductor. The transfer of heat from one point to another through a material is called conduction, and materials that allow this transfer are called conductors. This explains why cooking vessels are made of metal while their handles are made of wood or other materials that do not conduct heat. The section contains a student activity. Activity 4.3 has students immerse a metal spoon and a wooden spoon simultaneously in hot water and feel which spoon becomes hotter at its upper end.

4.1.5 Conduction of electricity extends the investigation of conductivity to electricity. The activity requires students to build a tester circuit (as in Chapter 3) and test various materials including aluminium foil, iron nail, sulfur, copper wire, coal, wood, stone, rubber eraser, and nylon rope. The observation that only metals make the bulb glow leads to the conclusion that metals are good conductors of electricity and non-metals are generally poor conductors. This explains why screwdriver handles and electrician's gloves are made of plastic or rubber. The section contains a student activity.

4.2 Effect of Air and Water on Metals: Iron investigates the conditions under which iron develops brown deposits (rust). A controlled experiment places iron nails in three conditions: dry air only, boiled water covered with oil (water only, no air), and open water in contact with air. Only the nail exposed to both water and air develops rust, demonstrating that moist air is responsible. The brown deposit is called rust and the process is called rusting. The broader deterioration of any metal's surface due to air, water, or other substances is called corrosion; examples include green coating on copper (verdigris) and black coating on silver. Methods to prevent rusting include painting, oiling, greasing, and galvanisation (applying a protective zinc layer). A Fascinating Facts box features the Iron Pillar of Delhi — more than 1,600 years old and still largely rust-free — as a testament to ancient Indian metallurgical skill. The section contains a student activity.

4.3 Effect of Air and Water on Other Metals demonstrates through a teacher-led activity that burning magnesium ribbon in air produces magnesium oxide, a white powder whose solution turns red litmus paper blue, confirming that oxides of metals are basic in nature. The section notes that sodium is so reactive it is stored in kerosene to prevent contact with oxygen and water. The section contains a student activity.

4.4 Substances that Behave Differently from Metals in Air and Water contrasts the behaviour of non-metals such as sulfur and phosphorus with metals. Burning sulfur in oxygen produces sulfur dioxide gas, which dissolves in water to form sulfurous acid, an acidic solution — establishing that oxides of non-metals are acidic in nature. Sulfur itself does not react with water. Phosphorus is so reactive it catches fire in atmospheric air and must be stored in water. Non-metals are characterised as generally soft, dull in appearance, neither malleable nor ductile, non-sonorous, and poor conductors of heat and electricity. A Dive Deeper box clarifies that metals and non-metals are sub-categories of elements — substances that cannot be broken down into simpler substances — and notes that 118 elements are currently known. Plastic, glass, wood, rubber, and paper are not classified as metals or non-metals because they are not elements. The section contains student activities.

4.5 Are Non-metals Essential in Everyday Life? challenges the impression that non-metals are unimportant by highlighting the vital roles of specific non-metals: oxygen is essential for all life; carbon is the building block of proteins, fats, and carbohydrates; nitrogen is used in fertilisers and is an essential plant nutrient; chlorine is used in water purification; iodine solution is applied as an antiseptic. A Science and Society box highlights the importance of metals and their alloys in everyday utensils, modern technologies, aerospace, and atomic energy, and notes that recycling of iron and aluminium in India helps minimise waste and support sustainability.

content.text:
CHAPTER SUMMARY:

Chapter 5 — Changes Around Us: Physical and Chemical opens with four students noticing changes in their everyday surroundings — ice melting into water, a rose bud blooming into a flower, a bottle of cold water warming up, and a banana developing more brown spots and a strong smell. These observations frame the central question: can the changes around us be sorted into meaningful categories? The chapter progressively builds the classification of changes into physical and chemical, examines reversibility, discusses desirability, and concludes with two slow natural change processes.

The introductory Activity 5.1 asks students to observe and record changes — including melting ice cubes, chopping vegetables, boiling water, making popcorn, cutting paper, burning wood, and drying wet clothes — and reflect on what is changing in each case, noting that changes may involve size, shape, smell, or other properties observed through the senses.

5.1 A Substance May Change in Appearance but Remain the Same! explores changes in which the underlying substance is not transformed into anything new. Through three sub-experiments in Activity 5.2 — folding paper into origami shapes, inflating and deflating a balloon, and crushing chalk into powder — students observe that the paper, rubber, and chalk remain the same substances even though their shape or size changed. The same principle connects to water existing in solid, liquid, and gaseous states while still being water. Changes in which only physical properties such as shape, size, and state change, and no new substance is formed, are defined as physical changes.

5.2 A Substance May Change in Appearance and Not Remain the Same! introduces chemical changes through a comparative experiment in Activity 5.3, in which students blow exhaled air through straws into tap water and lime water. Blowing into tap water produces only bubbles with no colour change, while blowing into lime water turns it milky due to the formation of insoluble calcium carbonate. Since a new substance is formed, this is identified as a chemical change brought about through a chemical reaction. The word equation is: Calcium hydroxide + Carbon dioxide → Calcium carbonate + Water. The section also contains Activity 5.4, in which vinegar (or lemon juice) is mixed with baking soda; the fizzing and gas produced turns lime water milky, confirming the gas is carbon dioxide — another chemical change: Vinegar + Baking soda → Carbon dioxide + Other substances.

5.3 Some Other Processes Involving Chemical Changes extends the concept of chemical change to three further phenomena, organised into two subsections.

5.3.1 Rusting revisits the formation of rust from Chapter 4, explicitly classifying it as a chemical change because a new substance — iron oxide — is formed.

5.3.2 Combustion identifies the burning of magnesium ribbon as a chemical change because a new white substance, magnesium oxide, is formed along with heat and light. A chemical reaction in which a substance reacts with oxygen and produces heat and/or light is defined as combustion, and the substances that undergo it are called combustible substances — examples include wood, paper, cotton, and kerosene. Activity 5.5 establishes that oxygen from air supports combustion by showing that a candle covered by a glass tumbler goes out while the uncovered one continues to burn; the carbon dioxide trapped inside can be confirmed with lime water. The sub-section then addresses whether air alone is sufficient for combustion, introducing the concept of ignition temperature — the minimum temperature at which a substance catches fire — through Activity 5.6, in which sunrays focused through a magnifying glass ignite paper. The conclusion is that combustion requires three things simultaneously, represented by the fire triangle: a combustible substance (fuel), oxygen, and heat sufficient to reach the ignition temperature. A Science and Society box explains that wrapping a cloth around a person whose clothes are on fire cuts off air supply and extinguishes the fire. A Fascinating Facts box introduces bioluminescence — the production of light without heat by fireflies through a chemical change.

5.4 Can Physical and Chemical Changes Occur in the Same Process? uses the burning candle as a case study to show that both types of change can co-exist in a single process. Activity 5.7 presents student dialogue about the burning candle. The chapter explains that the melting, flow, solidification, and evaporation of wax are physical changes, while the burning of wax vapour to produce new substances is a chemical change. A Know a Scientist feature profiles Michael Faraday, who delivered the famous lecture series Chemical History of a Candle in the nineteenth century to illustrate physical and chemical processes.

5.5 Are Changes Permanent? introduces the concept of reversibility. Activity 5.8 asks students to revisit the changes from Activity 5.1 and determine which can be reversed. The section establishes that some changes can be reversed — ice melting can be reversed by refreezing, and evaporated water can be condensed — while others cannot be reversed, such as chopping vegetables or making popcorn. Changes are thus grouped into reversible and irreversible changes.

5.6 Are All Changes Desirable? distinguishes changes that are useful or beneficial (desirable), such as ripening of fruits, cooking food, or converting food waste into compost, from those that cause harm or inconvenience (undesirable), such as rusting or food decay. The section also highlights the long-term environmental impact of human-driven changes: increased burning of fuels raises atmospheric carbon dioxide levels, and drying paints release substances that cause atmospheric pollution.

5.7 Some Slow Natural Changes examines two natural processes that involve both physical and chemical changes but unfold over very long time scales.

5.7.1 Weathering of rocks explains that large rocks break down into smaller pieces called sediments through physical changes driven by temperature variation, growing tree roots, and water freezing in cracks. Additionally, water and dissolved chemicals can react with rock surfaces, producing chemical changes in their composition; an example is basalt, which contains iron and develops a red iron oxide layer when exposed to water vapour or air over time. The combined physical and chemical breakdown of rocks is called weathering and eventually leads to the formation of soil.

5.7.2 Erosion describes the process by which rock pebbles, soil, and sediments are broken down and carried from one location to another by natural forces such as wind and flowing water. This is classified as a physical change. Sediments that settle in water bodies eventually harden into new rocks, a process that takes thousands of years and cannot be reversed.

content.text:
CHAPTER SUMMARY:

Chapter 6 — Adolescence: A Stage of Growth and Change opens by drawing a parallel between the growth of a plant — from seed to sapling to a plant capable of producing new seeds — and the growth of animals and humans, who must also mature before they can reproduce. The chapter maps the human life journey through infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood, and old age, establishes that adolescence typically spans ages 10 to 19 and is a period of rapid physical, biological, and emotional change, and guides students to understand these changes responsibly.

6.1 Growing With Age: The Teenage Years introduces the concept of adolescence through a conversation between two cousins, Venkatesh and Devyani, who notice changes in each other — a thin moustache, a changed voice, and increased height. The section defines adolescence as the stage of development between childhood and adulthood, generally starting around age 10 and continuing until 19. It then describes the most commonly observable physical changes occurring during this period. Increase in height becomes more prominent during adolescence even though height growth is continuous from birth. Changes in body structure, weight gain, and strength describe how boys may experience broader shoulders and wider chests while girls experience changes in height, weight, and breast development. Changes in voice explain that growth of the voice box (larynx) leads to a hoarse voice in boys, visible as the Adam's apple, while girls experience only slight voice changes as their voice box grows more slowly. Appearance of hair in different parts of the body notes that both boys and girls develop hair in the armpits and pubic region, while boys additionally develop facial hair in the form of moustaches and beards; variations in the timing of these changes are completely normal. Changes in facial skin: emergence of pimples explains that increased oily secretions from skin pores during adolescence can cause the skin condition acne, of which pimples are a manifestation, typically appearing on the face. The section introduces the term secondary sexual characteristics for changes that help distinguish males from females but are not directly involved in reproduction, and defines puberty as the stage in which the body undergoes external and internal changes to develop into an adult capable of reproduction. The section contains a student activity. Activity 6.1 asks students to anonymously write down changes they observe among classmates from Grades 5 to 8 related to height, strength, behaviour, or appearance, place the slips in a jar, and discuss the most commonly noted changes as a class.

6.2 Changes that Indicate Reproductive Capability covers internal changes associated with adolescence, particularly those related to reproductive maturation. In adolescent girls, a key internal change is the onset of the menstrual cycle, a recurring cycle of approximately 28 to 30 days (though a healthy range of 21 to 35 days is also noted) associated with reproductive health. The phase during which blood discharge occurs is called menstruation, which may last three to seven days. Menstruation begins at puberty and typically ends naturally between ages 45 and 55. A Breaking Myths about Menstruation box addresses the widespread social taboos and myths — including physical isolation of menstruating girls — that have no scientific basis, and encourages a scientific outlook to support reproductive health and a healthier lifestyle for women.

6.3 Emotional and Behavioural Changes in Adolescents establishes that adolescence involves not only physical changes but also heightened emotions and behavioural shifts. Adolescents may experience mood swings, strong emotions, and increased sensitivity, which can express themselves through engagement in music, dance, sports, or social activities. Understanding the relationship between emotions and behaviour helps adolescents respond thoughtfully to situations. The section contains a student activity. Activity 6.2 asks students to reflect on emotional and behavioural changes they or their classmates have experienced over the past year or two, and to complete Table 6.2 identifying key emotional changes, their probable effects on behaviour, and constructive ways to channel them.

6.4 Making Adolescence a Joyful Experience addresses four practical dimensions of healthy adolescent living, each covered in a subsection.

6.4.1 Meeting nutritional needs emphasises that adolescence, as a period of rapid physical change, requires an especially nutritious diet rich in proteins, carbohydrates, fats, vitamins, and minerals. Calcium from milk, millets, curd, cheese, and paneer supports optimal bone growth, proteins and carbohydrates support strength and energy, and iron from spinach, kidney beans, and dried fruits is essential for blood formation. A Science and Society box highlights that adolescent girls are particularly susceptible to blood-related health problems due to iron or Vitamin B12 deficiency, and invites students to explore government schemes addressing these deficiencies. A Know a Scientist feature profiles Dorothy Hodgkin, who determined the structure of Vitamin B12 and was the third woman to win the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1964. The section contains a student activity.

6.4.2 Personal hygiene explains that maintaining body hygiene — particularly in the armpits and pubic region — is important during adolescence to prevent infections. For girls, maintaining menstrual hygiene using sanitary pads or reusable cloth pads is essential for both comfort and health. Used sanitary pads should be wrapped and disposed of in a dustbin. A Science and Society box describes four government schemes to support menstrual hygiene: the Menstrual Hygiene Scheme (MHS), which provides sanitary pads free or at reduced cost in rural areas; the Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram (RKSK), which promotes peer education on menstrual health; the Suvidha Sanitary Napkin Initiative, which provides biodegradable pads through Jan Aushadhi Kendras; and various State-Level Initiatives such as the Shuchi Scheme in Karnataka and free napkin distribution in Tamil Nadu and Odisha.

6.4.3 Physical activities establishes that regular exercise and participation in games and sports during adolescence keeps the body and mind healthy, builds stamina, and improves mood, making physical activity an essential part of adolescent wellness.

6.4.4 Balanced social life emphasises that adolescents should be polite and respectful in their interactions both in person and online, and should use social media platforms responsibly. A Science and Society box on cyberbullying defines it as the use of digital devices to harass others through misleading messages, false rumours, or sharing personal information without consent, and advises students to seek help from parents or teachers if bullied rather than responding with fear. The section contains a student activity. Activity 6.4 asks students to work in groups to design posters and pamphlets about responsible social media behaviour and to complete a dos and don'ts table (Table 6.4).

6.4.5 Avoiding harmful substances — learn to say NO addresses the risk of peer pressure to try addictive substances such as tobacco, gutka, cigarettes, beedi, alcohol, and illegal drugs during adolescence. The section explains that these substances are addictive, meaning that once consumed, they create a compulsive urge to continue, a pattern called substance abuse. Health consequences include breathing difficulties, memory loss, and lung damage. The section urges students to confidently say no and seek support from family, friends, or counsellors if needed. A Science and Society box describes the Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan, a government initiative focused on spreading awareness about substance abuse prevention, particularly among early-age children, and mentions the National De-addiction Helpline number 14446.

6.5 The 'Why' Question for Adolescence addresses the underlying biological cause of the changes described throughout the chapter. The key concept introduced is that of hormones — chemical substances produced in different parts of the body, released in response to signals from the brain, that regulate growth, development, reproduction, and behaviour. Puberty, menstruation, and mood changes during adolescence are all primarily driven by hormonal activity. The chapter closes by affirming that staying informed, seeking support, and making healthy decisions helps adolescents build a strong foundation for life ahead.

content.text:
CHAPTER SUMMARY:

Chapter 7 — Heat Transfer in Nature opens with siblings Pema and Palden sitting around a fireplace in Gangtok on a winter evening. Their conversation — about why Kerala is warmer than Sikkim and why cooking utensils are made of metal — launches the chapter's inquiry into the three modes of heat transfer: conduction, convection, and radiation. The chapter then extends these ideas to natural large-scale phenomena, including land and sea breezes, the water cycle, and groundwater seepage.

7.1 Conduction of Heat establishes through an experimental investigation that heat travels along a metal strip from its hotter end towards its cooler end. The process of heat transfer from the hotter part of an object to the cooler part, where the particles themselves do not move from their positions but pass heat on to neighbouring particles, is defined as conduction. Materials that allow heat to pass through them easily — such as metals — are called good conductors of heat, and this explains why cooking utensils are made of metal. Materials such as glass, wood, clay, and porcelain do not allow heat to pass through easily and are called poor conductors or insulators of heat; this is why clay and porcelain cups keep tea or coffee hot for longer. Air is also a poor conductor of heat, which is why woollen clothes (whose fibres trap air in their pores) keep us warm in winter and why two thin blankets are warmer than one thick blanket of the same total thickness. A Fascinating Facts box describes traditional houses in the Mori block of Uttarkashi (Himalayas), whose walls consist of two wooden layers filled with cow dung and mud — both poor conductors — to retain warmth. Hollow bricks used in modern construction serve the same purpose. The section contains a student activity. Activity 7.1 directs students to attach four wax-held pins at equal intervals on a metal strip, heat one end, predict the order in which pins will fall, and record observations.

7.2 Convection addresses how heat is transferred through fluids — both liquids and gases. The observation of smoke rising from burning firewood motivates the investigation. Because air near a flame heats up, expands, becomes lighter, and rises, cooler air moves in to take its place, establishing a circulating current. This process of heat transfer by the actual movement of particles of a liquid or gas is defined as convection. The section confirms through a potassium permanganate experiment in heated water that liquids also transfer heat by convection: heated water at the base expands, becomes lighter, and rises, while cooler water from the sides descends, creating a visible circulation loop. The section contains student activities.

7.2.1 Land and Sea Breeze extends convection to the meteorological scale. Because land heats up faster than water during the day, warm air above the land rises and cooler air from the sea moves in to replace it; this movement of cooler air from sea to land is called a sea breeze. At night the process reverses — land cools faster than water, so air above the sea is now warmer and rises, and cooler air moves from the land towards the sea, producing a land breeze. This explains why people in coastal areas experience a reversal of wind direction between day and night, and why houses in coastal areas are built with windows facing the sea. The section contains a student activity. Activity 7.4 asks students to compare the rates of heating and cooling of soil and water by placing thermometers in two bowls set in sunlight and recording temperature every five minutes.

7.3 Radiation identifies the third mode of heat transfer as radiation — the process by which heat travels directly from a hot object to cooler surroundings without requiring any material medium. This is how heat from the Sun reaches the Earth across space, and how warmth from a fireplace reaches people sitting near it. All objects radiate heat; a hot utensil removed from a flame eventually cools because it radiates heat to its surroundings. A Dive Deeper box explains that light-coloured clothes reflect most heat and are therefore more comfortable in summer, while dark-coloured clothes absorb more heat and are preferred in winter. The section notes that in many everyday situations — such as water being heated in a pan — all three processes operate simultaneously: heat passes from the flame to the metal pan by conduction, water inside heats up by convection, and the warmth felt around the flame and hot pan is due to radiation. A Fascinating Facts box describes the bukhari, a traditional iron stove used in the Himalayan region for cooking and room heating, which involves all three modes of heat transfer.

7.4 Water Cycle connects heat transfer, specifically solar radiation and evaporation, to the continuous movement of water on Earth. Water exists in three states in nature: as liquid in oceans, rivers, and lakes; as solid snow, ice sheets, and glaciers in mountains and polar regions; and as water vapour in the atmosphere. Solar radiation drives evaporation from water bodies and transpiration from plants, converting liquid water into water vapour that rises into the atmosphere. As it rises and cools, it condenses to form clouds, which return water to the Earth's surface through precipitation as rain, snow, or hail. The continuous movement of water upward as vapour and downward through precipitation, passing through soil, rocks, and plants and finally returning to water bodies, is called the water cycle. A Know a Scientist feature profiles Varahamihira, a sixth-century CE astronomer and mathematician from Ujjaini, whose work Brihatsamhita gave methods for predicting seasonal rainfall based on observations of cloud formation, wind patterns, and celestial phenomena.

7.4.1 Seepage of water beneath the Earth investigates how rainfall that reaches the Earth's surface seeps downward through soil and rock. Water seeps fastest through gravel, slower through sand, and slowest through clay, because the spaces between particles are largest in gravel and most interconnected. The process of surface water seeping through soil and rocks is called infiltration. Water that seeps through and accumulates in the pore spaces of sediments and openings in rocks beneath the surface is called groundwater. The underground layers of sediments and rocks that store groundwater are called aquifers, which are accessed by wells and bore wells. The section notes that groundwater is being depleted by excessive extraction and reduced infiltration due to increased urban concretisation, and that rainwater harvesting and recharge pits help replenish groundwater. content.text:
CHAPTER SUMMARY:

Chapter 8 — Measurement of Time and Motion opens with Prerna, a district-level 100 metre sprint champion, watching Olympic race footage and marvelling at how precisely time is measured in modern sports compared to the humble stopwatch at her school. Her curiosity about how time was measured before clocks and watches existed frames the chapter's two-part investigation: first, the history and science of timekeeping culminating in the pendulum and the SI unit of time; and second, the concepts of speed and types of linear motion.

8.1 Measurement of Time traces the development of timekeeping from ancient observations of repeating natural events — the rising and setting of the Sun, lunar phases, and changing seasons — to the invention of mechanical clocks. Early human civilisations used these natural cycles to create calendars, defining a day by the Sun's rising and setting. To measure smaller intervals within a day, they devised sundials (where a shadow's position marks the time), two types of water clocks (the outflow type, where water drains from a marked vessel, and the floating bowl or Ghatika-yantra type, where a bowl with a fine hole slowly fills and sinks), hourglasses (where sand flows from one bulb to another), and candle clocks (candles with time-indicating markings). A Fascinating Facts box highlights the Samrat Yantra at the Jantar Mantar in Jaipur, Rajasthan — the world's largest stone sundial, built around 300 years ago, whose 27-metre-high shadow moves at about 1 millimetre per second and can measure intervals as short as 2 seconds. A second Fascinating Facts box describes ancient Indian timekeeping: shadow-based methods referenced in Kautilya's Arthasastra (second century BCE–third century CE), Varahamihira's accurate shadow formulations around 530 CE, and the Ghatika-yantra mentioned by Aryabhata and used continuously at Buddhist monasteries, royal palaces, and town squares until the late nineteenth century, with each sinking cycle lasting 24 minutes (one ghatika or ghati), giving 60 ghatis to a day. The development of mechanical clocks driven by weights, gears, and springs from the fourteenth century onwards led to the invention of the pendulum clock. A Know a Scientist feature profiles Christiaan Huygens (1629–1695), who invented the pendulum clock in 1656–1657, building on Galileo Galilei's (1564–1642) discovery that the time for each swing of a pendulum is constant. The section contains a student activity. Activity 8.1 guides students to construct a simple water clock from a cut plastic bottle, calibrate it by marking water levels at one-minute intervals, and use it to measure short time intervals.

8.1.1 A simple pendulum introduces the pendulum as a device consisting of a small metallic ball (the bob) suspended by a long thread from a rigid support. At rest, the bob hangs at its mean position. When displaced and released, it swings back and forth in oscillatory motion that is periodic — it repeats its path after a fixed interval of time. One oscillation is defined as the motion of the bob from the mean position to one extreme position, then to the other extreme position, and back to the mean position. The time taken to complete one oscillation is defined as the time period of the pendulum. Through Activity 8.2, students measure the time taken for 10 oscillations of a pendulum of 100 cm string length and calculate the time period by dividing by 10; repeated trials show the time period is nearly constant. A Think Like a Scientist box guides further investigations to establish that the time period of a pendulum depends on its length but not on the mass of the bob, and that all pendulums of the same length at the same location have the same time period. This constancy is the property exploited in mechanical timekeeping. All clocks — ancient or modern — are based on some process repeating continuously at equal time intervals. A Dive Deeper box notes that modern quartz clocks use the vibrations of a quartz crystal, and atomic clocks use vibrations of specific atoms; today's atomic clocks lose only one second in millions of years.

8.1.2 SI unit of time establishes that the SI unit of time is the second, with symbol s. Larger units are the minute (min; 60 s = 1 min) and the hour (h; 60 min = 1 h). A Dive Deeper box clarifies writing conventions for units: time unit names and symbols are written in lowercase letters, no full stop after the symbol, a space between the number and unit, and the abbreviations 'sec' and 'hrs' are incorrect. A Fascinating Facts box reinforces that the Ghatika-yantra established the ghatika as the standard time unit in India until the nineteenth century. The section contains a student activity. Activity 8.3 asks students to examine a wall clock and identify the smallest time interval it can measure, establishing that one second is the smallest measurable interval on a standard wall clock. A Science and Society box describes precision timekeeping in sports (milliseconds), medicine (ECG machines measuring millisecond heartbeat variations), music (digital recordings capturing thousands of samples per second), and computing (smartphones and computers processing signals in microseconds).

8.2 Slow or Fast transitions from timekeeping to the concept of comparing motion. The section uses the example of runners in a straight-line race: to decide who is faster when all run the same distance, one measures the time taken; a runner who covers the same distance in less time is moving faster. The section extends this to comparing motions over different distances, motivating the need for a single combined measure of how fast or slow an object moves.

8.3 Speed defines speed as the distance covered by an object in unit time. The formula is: Speed = Total distance covered ÷ Total time taken. The SI unit of speed is metre per second (m/s); when distance is in kilometres and time in hours, speed is expressed in kilometre per hour (km/h). Three worked examples (Examples 8.1, 8.2, and 8.3) practise calculating speed, distance, and time from given quantities. A Science and Society box describes the speedometer (which measures and displays a vehicle's speed in km/h) and the odometer (which measures the total distance travelled) as instruments fitted in most vehicles. The section contains a student activity. Activity 8.4 asks students to look up a railway timetable, identify trains near their locality, and calculate and compare the speeds of different train types (Passenger, Express, Superfast) between two stations.

8.3.1 Relationship between speed, distance, and time formalises the three rearrangements of the speed formula: Speed = Distance ÷ Time; Distance = Speed × Time; Time = Distance ÷ Speed. Additional worked examples reinforce the use of each form. The section also introduces the term average speed for the speed calculated over the entire journey, noting that in reality objects rarely move at exactly constant speed throughout.

8.4 Uniform and Non-uniform Linear Motion revisits the concept of linear motion from Grade 6 — motion along a straight line — and introduces two types. When an object moving along a straight line covers equal distances in equal intervals of time, it is in uniform linear motion. When its speed keeps changing so that it covers unequal distances in equal time intervals, it is in non-uniform linear motion. A tabulated data set for two trains, X and Y, travelling between the same two stations in the same overall time demonstrates that Train X, covering 20 km in every 10-minute interval, is in uniform linear motion, while Train Y, whose per-interval distances vary, is in non-uniform linear motion. The section notes that uniform linear motion is an idealisation; in everyday life, most motion is non-uniform, which is why average speeds are used. A Fascinating Facts box closes the chapter by reflecting that, despite our ability to measure time with extraordinary precision, the fundamental nature of time remains a deep philosophical and scientific question.

CHAPTER SUMMARY:

9.1 Nutrition in Animals

Animals obtain energy from food by breaking down complex components such as carbohydrates, proteins, and fats into simpler, absorbable forms through a process called digestion. This breakdown takes place along a long continuous tube called the alimentary canal, which runs from the mouth to the anus. The simpler molecules produced through digestion are absorbed into the blood and transported to every cell in the body to fuel life processes.

9.1.1 Digestion in human beings

This subsection traces the step-by-step journey of food through the human alimentary canal, explaining how each organ contributes to the progressive breakdown and absorption of nutrients.

Beginning with the mouth cavity

Digestion begins in the mouth, where teeth perform mechanical digestion by crushing and grinding food into smaller pieces. Saliva, produced by salivary glands in the mouth, contains a digestive juice that chemically breaks down starch into simpler sugars — which is why starchy foods like chapati or rice taste sweeter when chewed for a long time. The chapter includes Activity 9.1, in which students test boiled rice for the presence of starch using iodine solution, comparing unchewed rice to rice that has been thoroughly chewed, to observe starch breakdown in the mouth.

Food pipe (Oesophagus): A passage from the mouth to the stomach

Once food is chewed, saliva moistens it into a soft ball and the tongue pushes it into the oesophagus, a long flexible muscular tube that connects the mouth cavity to the stomach. The walls of the oesophagus contract and relax in rhythmic wave-like movements that push the food downward; this motion continues throughout the entire length of the alimentary canal.

Stomach

In the stomach, the muscular walls contract and relax to churn the food and mix it thoroughly with a secretion containing digestive juice, acid, and mucus. The digestive juice breaks down proteins, the acid kills harmful bacteria that may have entered with the food, and the mucus protects the stomach's own lining from being damaged by the acid. Food remains in the stomach until it is reduced to a semi-liquid mass before passing to the next stage.

Small Intestine

The partially digested food moves into the small intestine, which is approximately 6 metres long and is the longest part of the alimentary canal. The small intestine receives digestive secretions from three sources: its own inner lining, the liver (which secretes bile to neutralise the acidic food mass and to help break down fats), and the pancreas (which secretes pancreatic juice to further break down carbohydrates, proteins, and fats). The inner lining of the small intestine carries thousands of tiny finger-like projections that greatly increase its surface area; through these projections, digested nutrients are absorbed into the blood vessels in the intestinal wall and transported to the rest of the body, a process the chapter calls absorption.

Large intestine

Undigested material that the small intestine cannot absorb passes into the large intestine, which is about 1.5 metres long and considerably wider than the small intestine. Here, water and some salts are absorbed from the remaining material, which gradually becomes solid waste called stool. The stool is stored in the rectum until it is expelled from the body through the anus, a process called egestion.

9.1.2 Do all animals digest food the same way as humans do?

Animals show considerable variation in their digestive adaptations depending on their diet and feeding habits. Grass-eating animals such as cows and buffaloes are called ruminants; they quickly swallow partially chewed grass, store it in a part of their stomach, and later return it to the mouth to chew it thoroughly before swallowing again — a process called rumination or chewing the cud. Birds do not have teeth and therefore cannot chew food; instead they have a muscular chamber called the gizzard in which food is broken down by powerful contractions of its walls, sometimes aided by small stones the birds swallow deliberately.

9.2 Respiration in Animals

The nutrients absorbed from food must be converted into usable energy inside the body's cells, and this conversion is achieved through respiration. The chapter draws a clear distinction between breathing and respiration: breathing is the physical act of moving air in and out of the lungs, whereas respiration is the chemical process by which oxygen reacts with glucose inside cells to release carbon dioxide, water, and energy.

9.2.1 Respiration in humans

How do we breathe?

The human respiratory system consists of the nostrils, nasal passages, windpipe, and two lungs, working together to bring fresh air into the body and expel waste gases. Air inhaled through the nostrils passes through the nasal passages, where fine hairs and mucus filter out dust and dirt, before travelling down the windpipe into the lungs; inside the lungs the windpipe branches repeatedly into smaller passages that end in millions of tiny balloon-like sacs called alveoli. The chapter includes Activity 9.2, in which students construct a model using a plastic bottle and balloons to observe how changes in the volume of the chest cavity drive the movement of air in and out of the lungs, demonstrating the role of the diaphragm and rib muscles. During inhalation the ribs move upward and outward while the dome-shaped diaphragm moves downward, increasing the volume of the chest cavity so that air rushes in; during exhalation the ribs move down and inward and the diaphragm moves upward, compressing the cavity and pushing air out.

What do we breathe out?

Activity 9.3 demonstrates that exhaled air contains a higher concentration of carbon dioxide than inhaled air, confirmed when exhaled air causes lime water to turn milky while inhaled air does not. Inhaled air contains approximately 21% oxygen and 0.04% carbon dioxide, whereas exhaled air contains 16–17% oxygen and 4–5% carbon dioxide, showing that the body consumes oxygen and produces carbon dioxide during respiration.

How does the exchange of gases happen?

Gas exchange between air and blood takes place in the alveoli, which have extremely thin walls surrounded by a dense network of fine blood vessels. Blood arriving at the alveoli carries carbon dioxide collected from the body's cells; this carbon dioxide passes into the air inside the alveoli and is breathed out, while oxygen from freshly inhaled air passes in the opposite direction into the blood and is carried to all tissues of the body. The word equation given for this process is: Glucose + Oxygen → Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy.

9.2.2 Do other animals breathe the same way as humans do?

While many animals — including birds, mammals such as elephants and lions, and reptiles such as snakes — breathe through lungs, the precise structure of their lungs varies across groups. Aquatic animals such as fish breathe through gills, which are richly supplied with blood vessels that allow dissolved oxygen in the surrounding water to pass into the blood and carbon dioxide from the blood to pass out into the water. Frogs and other amphibians use gills for breathing as tadpoles, develop lungs for life on land as adults, and can also exchange gases through their moist skin when in water; earthworms, which have no specialised respiratory organs, exchange gases entirely through their moist skin surface.

content.text:
CHAPTER SUMMARY:

Chapter 10 — Life Processes in Plants connects to Grade 6 learning that all living beings need food for growth, and to Chapter 9's discussion of how animals obtain nutrition. The chapter opens with the question of how plants — which do not eat food as animals do — obtain the nutrients they need. The four major sections progressively establish that plants make their own food through photosynthesis using sunlight, water, carbon dioxide, and chlorophyll; transport water and food through xylem and phloem respectively; and, like all living organisms, also respire to release energy. A Fascinating Facts box quotes from the ancient Indian text Vrikshayurveda, which recorded practical observations on plant growth, soil, and agricultural practices including methods of organic manure preparation.

10.1 How Do Plants Grow? builds on prior knowledge that plants require water and sunlight, testing these claims through a controlled experiment. The section contains a student activity. Activity 10.1 asks students to set up three pots with similar saplings under different conditions — Pot A in sunlight with water, Pot B in sunlight without water, and Pot C in the dark with water — observe changes in height, number of leaves, and leaf colour over two weeks, and infer that plants require both sunlight and water for healthy growth.

10.2 How Do Plants Get Food for their Growth? explores the mechanism by which plants synthesise their own food, organised into four subsections.

10.2.1 Leaves: the 'food factories' of plants introduces the concept that plants store food in the form of starch and that starch is produced in the leaves. Leaves are typically broad and flat, and are mostly green due to the presence of a pigment called chlorophyll, which efficiently captures sunlight. The iodine test — turning a decolourised leaf blue-black if starch is present — is introduced as a method to detect starch. Activity 10.2 is a teacher-led demonstration in which a leaf is first boiled in water, then in alcohol (to remove chlorophyll and enable observation of colour change), before being tested with dilute iodine solution; a blue-black colour indicates the presence of starch. Activity 10.3 investigates the relationship between chlorophyll, sunlight, and starch production using leaves with green and non-green patches from plants kept in sunlight and in the dark; the result shows that only green patches of sunlit plants test positive for starch, confirming that chlorophyll and sunlight are both essential for starch preparation, and that leaves are therefore the food factories of plants. A Fascinating Facts box notes that some plant leaves appear red, violet, or brown because they contain more of these coloured pigments than green chlorophyll; these pigments also assist in photosynthesis, and starch can be detected in such leaves using the iodine test.

10.2.2 Role of air in the preparation of food investigates which gas from the air is essential for food preparation. The section contains a student activity. Activity 10.4 is a teacher-led demonstration in which half a leaf of a destarched plant is placed inside a bottle containing sodium hydroxide solution (which absorbs carbon dioxide from the air), while the other half remains outside. After placing the setup in sunlight and conducting a starch test, only the half outside the bottle turns blue-black, showing that carbon dioxide from the air is essential for the plant to prepare starch. The section concludes that four things — sunlight, water, chlorophyll, and carbon dioxide — are all essential for the synthesis of food in plants, and names this process photosynthesis.

10.2.3 Photosynthesis: in a nutshell consolidates the process of photosynthesis. Food is produced in the form of glucose (a simple carbohydrate), which serves as an instant energy source and is later converted to starch for storage. The word equation of photosynthesis is: Carbon dioxide + Water → (in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll) → Glucose + Oxygen. Other green parts of the plant besides leaves that contain chlorophyll also perform photosynthesis. A Know a Scientist feature profiles Rustom Hormusji Dastur (1896–1961), an Indian plant scientist who studied the effects of water, temperature, and light colour on photosynthesis and headed the Botany Department at the Royal Institute of Science, Bombay. Activity 10.5 investigates the gas released during photosynthesis using an aquatic plant in a beaker of water; set-up A placed in sunlight produces gas bubbles that accumulate in an inverted test tube, and a glowing splint introduced into the tube bursts into flame, confirming that oxygen is released during photosynthesis, which only occurs in sunlight.

10.2.4 How do leaves exchange gases during photosynthesis? introduces the structural feature that enables leaves to take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen. Activity 10.6 is a demonstration in which a thin peel from the lower surface of a leaf (such as rhoeo, money plant, or onion) is placed on a microscope slide and examined under a microscope; students observe numerous tiny pores called stomata. Stomata, present on the surface of leaves, facilitate the exchange of gases during both photosynthesis and respiration.

10.3 Transport in Plants examines how substances move within a plant, covered in two subsections.

10.3.1 Transport of water and minerals explains that roots absorb water and dissolved minerals from the soil and that these must be transported to leaves and other parts of the plant. Activity 10.7 demonstrates this by placing a stem cutting in red-inked water; after one day, the red colour is visible in the stem, leaves, and flowers. Cutting the stem and examining it with a magnifying glass reveals red-coloured tube-like structures called xylem present in the stem, branches, and leaves of plants. Water and minerals dissolved in water travel upward through the xylem.

10.3.2 Transport of food explains that the food prepared in the leaves during photosynthesis must also be transported to all parts of the plant, including roots, stems, and seeds where it may be stored. This food is transported through a different set of thin tube-like structures called phloem.

10.4 Do Plants Respire? addresses the question of whether plants, like animals, also carry out respiration. Activity 10.8 is a teacher-led demonstration in which germinating moong bean seeds are sealed in a conical flask for 24 hours; gas channelled from the flask through rubber tubing into lime water turns the lime water milky, confirming that the seeds have released carbon dioxide. This demonstrates that plants (and their seeds) respire. During respiration, glucose is broken down in the presence of oxygen, releasing carbon dioxide, water, and energy: Glucose + Oxygen → Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy. The energy released is used for plant growth and development. All parts of a plant — both green and non-green — carry out respiration. The chapter concludes by affirming that plants have distinct mechanisms for synthesising food (photosynthesis), transporting it (through xylem and phloem), and releasing energy from it (respiration). A Know a Scientist feature profiles Kamala Sohonie (1911–1998), who received a Ph.D. from Cambridge University for her work on respiration in plants and later became Director of the Royal Institute of Science, Bombay; much of her work improved the nutritive value of plant foods and she investigated the sap of the coconut palm as a nutritive drink called Neera.

ARUVI — CLOSING SYNTHESIS RE-AUTHORING · SCIENCE · MIDDLE STAGE

You are re-writing ONE unit: the closing whole-chapter synthesis of a chapter's fullest
lesson plan. This unit is served in two situations, and it must be excellent in both:

1. As the FINAL unit of the fullest plan — the class finishes the chapter with it.
2. As ONE EXTRA 40-minute period appended to a SHORTER complete plan of the same
   chapter, whose own final unit (given below) already consolidated the chapter
   yesterday.

THE UNIT YOU ARE WRITING closes the chapter through one fresh, concrete application: a
scenario, artefact, dataset, place or design problem the chapter itself never uses. The
class brings the chapter's concepts; the unit puts them to work in the new setting, and
what the task shows IS the synthesis — the chapter drawn together by using it whole, not
by summarising it.

PROPERTIES OF THE UNIT:
- It opens directly onto its fresh setting: the first band presents the new material and
  puts the first question to the class.
- Every concept or skill it calls on appears in EVERY unit-title map given below — the
  shorter plans differ in what they cover; write only to what all of them share.
