content.text:
CHAPTER SUMMARY:

Chapter 11 — Light: Shadows and Reflections opens with Reza and her grandmother preparing a shadow puppet performance using a diya (oil lamp) and cutout puppets, and noticing how the shadow of a hand changes when moved closer to or farther from the lamp. These everyday observations motivate the chapter's four core topics: sources of light, the straight-line travel of light, shadow formation and transparency, and the pinhole camera and reflection of light.

11.1 Sources of Light distinguishes between two categories of objects based on their relationship with light. Objects that produce their own light — such as the Sun, fire, burning diyas, candles, electric bulbs, LEDs, and glow-worms — are called luminous objects. Objects that do not produce their own light but are visible only because they reflect light falling on them — such as the Moon, tables, books, and people — are called non-luminous objects. The section contains a student activity. Activity 11.1 presents a list of objects and asks students to classify each as luminous or non-luminous by deciding whether it produces its own light. A Fascinating Facts box describes bioluminescence, the ability of certain living organisms — including some deep-sea fish such as the anglerfish, fireflies, glow-worms, and certain bacteria and fungi — to produce their own light through chemical reactions in their bodies.

11.2 Does Light Travel in a Straight Line? investigates the path taken by light using two activities. Activity 11.2 places three cardboard sheets each with a small hole in alignment, with a candle at one end; when the holes are aligned, the flame is visible, but when any card is shifted, the flame disappears. Activity 11.3 shines a torch through a straight hollow tube (where light passes through) and then through a bent tube (where no light emerges at the other end). Both activities lead to the conclusion that light always travels in a straight line. This property is called the rectilinear propagation of light, and a ray of light is represented diagrammatically as a straight line with an arrowhead showing the direction of travel.

11.3 Shadows establishes the conditions under which a shadow is formed. When an opaque object is placed in the path of light, it blocks the light and casts a dark region behind it — this dark region is called a shadow. The section uses this observation to classify materials on the basis of how much light they allow to pass through. Materials that allow almost all light to pass through and through which objects are clearly visible are called transparent — examples include clear glass, clean water, and air. Materials that do not allow any light to pass through are called opaque — examples include wood, metal, cardboard, and stone. Materials that allow some light to pass through but scatter it so that objects behind them appear blurry are called translucent — examples include frosted glass, butter paper, and thin cloth. The section also explores how the size of a shadow varies: moving the object closer to the light source makes the shadow larger, while moving it farther from the source or closer to the screen makes the shadow smaller. The section contains student activities. Activity 11.4 uses a torch to cast the shadow of a hand, varying the distance between the hand and the wall, to observe shadow size changes. Activity 11.5 asks students to classify a set of objects — including clear glass, wood, cardboard, a glass tumbler, thin cloth, and a plastic bag — as transparent, translucent, or opaque based on the clarity of the shadows they cast.

11.4 Pinhole Camera explains a simple device that demonstrates the rectilinear propagation of light. A pinhole camera consists of two nested boxes — an inner box with a small pinhole on one face and an outer box covered on the opposite side with tracing paper or translucent material as a screen. Light from an object enters through the tiny pinhole and forms an image on the screen inside. Because light from the top of the object travels in a straight line through the pinhole and reaches the bottom of the screen, and vice versa, the image formed is inverted (upside down). The section contains a student activity. Activity 11.6 guides students to construct a pinhole camera from two cardboard boxes, one sliding inside the other, make a pinhole on the outer closed face and the translucent screen on the open inner face, point it at a bright source or outdoor scene, and observe and sketch the image. A Fascinating Facts box describes the camera obscura, a large room-sized ancestor of the pinhole camera used by artists in the past to trace scenes, and notes that some early photographers used pinhole cameras to capture images on photographic paper.

11.5 Mirrors and Reflections covers the behaviour of light when it strikes a smooth, polished surface, organised into four subsections.

11.5.1 Reflection of light introduces reflection as the bouncing back of light when it strikes a surface. Activity 11.7 directs a torch beam at a mirror in a dark room and observes a reflected beam on the adjacent wall, establishing that smooth surfaces such as mirrors reflect light strongly, while rough or uneven surfaces scatter light in many directions without producing a clear reflected beam. Common examples of reflection in everyday life include seeing a reflection in still water or a polished metal surface.

11.5.2 Laws of reflection establishes the two fundamental laws governing how light reflects. The perpendicular to the mirror surface at the point of incidence is called the normal. The angle between the incoming ray (incident ray) and the normal is called the angle of incidence, and the angle between the reflected ray and the normal is called the angle of reflection. Activity 11.8 guides students to direct a ray of light at a mirror at various angles, trace the incident and reflected rays, measure both angles, and record results in a table. The observations establish the two laws of reflection: the angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection; and the incident ray, the normal, and the reflected ray all lie in the same plane. A Know a Scientist feature profiles Ibn al-Haytham (965–1040 CE), also known as Alhazen, an Arab scientist whose Book of Optics made foundational contributions to the understanding of vision, light, reflection, and refraction, establishing him as one of the founders of modern optics.

11.5.3 Image in a plane mirror investigates the nature and position of the image formed when an object is placed in front of a flat (plane) mirror. Activity 11.9 uses two identical pins and a plane mirror to locate the image of one pin by finding the point where the other pin exactly coincides with the reflected image. The key observations are that the image appears to be behind the mirror at the same distance as the object is in front, is the same size as the object, and cannot be formed on a screen — such an image is called a virtual image. The image in a plane mirror also appears laterally inverted, meaning the left side of the object appears as the right side of the image. Activity 11.10 demonstrates lateral inversion by writing text in front of a mirror and noting the reversed appearance; the word AMBULANCE on emergency vehicles is printed in reverse so that drivers ahead can read it correctly in their rear-view mirrors. A Fascinating Facts box describes the periscope, a device using two plane mirrors at 45° angles to allow observation over or around obstacles such as walls or submarine hulls.

11.5.4 Multiple reflections explores what happens when an object is placed between two mirrors. Activity 11.11 places an object between two plane mirrors held at different angles and observes multiple images formed by repeated reflections. When the mirrors are kept parallel to each other, the number of images becomes very large. The kaleidoscope is introduced as a device based on multiple reflections — three mirrors arranged in a triangular prism create multiple reflections of coloured beads or glass pieces, producing symmetrical and ever-changing patterns. Students are guided to construct a simple kaleidoscope.

content.text:
CHAPTER SUMMARY:

Chapter 12 — Earth, Moon, and the Sun opens with Rashmika, a 12-year-old in Kanniyakumari, who notices that coconut tree shadows are long in the morning and shorter in the afternoon. She wonders whether this happens because the Sun is moving across the sky, or because the Earth itself is moving. The chapter addresses this question by investigating the Earth's rotation and revolution, the phenomena of seasons, and the formation of solar and lunar eclipses.

12.1 Rotation of the Earth introduces the Earth's rotation through the analogy of riding a merry-go-round: a person sitting on a merry-go-round rotating anti-clockwise sees the surrounding trees and objects appearing to rotate clockwise. In the same way, the Sun appears to rise in the East and move westward across the sky not because the Sun is moving, but because the Earth itself is rotating from West to East. The Earth spins on its own axis — an imaginary line passing through its geographic North Pole and South Pole — and completes one full rotation in approximately 24 hours. When viewed from above the North Pole, the Earth rotates in the anti-clockwise direction, that is, from West to East. A Dive Deeper box defines rotation as the motion of an object in which all its parts move in circles around an imaginary line (the axis of rotation) passing through it. The rotation of the Earth from West to East causes the day-night cycle: the side of the Earth facing the Sun experiences daytime, and the opposite side experiences night. As Earth rotates, locations move alternately into sunlight and darkness, producing sunrise and sunset. The section contains student activities. Activity 12.1 uses a merry-go-round to help students experience how rotation causes surrounding objects to appear to move in the opposite direction. Activity 12.2 uses a globe, a small sticker to mark the student's location, and a torch to demonstrate how one half of the Earth is illuminated at any time, and how rotating the globe from West to East produces the cycle of day and night. Activity 12.3 asks students to observe the Big Dipper (Saptarishi) constellation over several hours at night and notice that it appears to move around the Pole Star (Dhruva Tara). Since the Earth's axis of rotation points very close to the Pole Star, that star appears nearly stationary, while all other stars appear to circle around it, rising in the East and setting in the West. The Moon also rises in the East and sets in the West for the same reason. A Fascinating Facts box describes the Foucault pendulum, a long pendulum with a heavy bob whose swinging plane appears to rotate over time, providing simple proof of the Earth's rotation. A 22-metre Foucault pendulum hangs from the skylight of the Constitution Hall in India's new Parliament building in New Delhi. A second Fascinating Facts box describes star trails — circular arcs recorded when astrophotographers keep camera shutters open for a long time — as a visual record of apparent star motion due to Earth's rotation. A third Fascinating Facts box highlights Aryabhata (fifth century CE), whose treatise Aryabhatiya contained a verse explaining that the apparent westward movement of stars is caused by the eastward rotation of the Earth; his calculated value for the Earth's rotation period was approximately 23 hours, 56 minutes, and 4.1 seconds — impressively close to the currently accepted value.

12.2 Revolution of the Earth establishes that while the Earth rotates on its own axis, it also simultaneously revolves around the Sun. Revolution is defined as the motion of an object around another object, and the path an object takes while revolving is called its orbit. The Earth's orbit around the Sun is nearly circular when viewed from above, and the Earth completes one revolution in approximately 365 days and 6 hours.

12.2.1 Changing view of night sky from the Earth explains that as the Earth revolves around the Sun, the direction in which we face at night (away from the Sun) gradually changes over the year. Consequently, different stars and constellations are visible at different times of the year — stars that rise at sunset in March are different from those that rise at sunset in September. This is why certain constellations are associated with particular seasons. A Fascinating Facts box notes that the Bhil and Pawara communities of the Tapi Valley in western India traditionally used the appearance of specific star patterns in the sky as indicators of the approaching monsoon season.

12.2.2 Seasons on the Earth explains that the Earth's axis of rotation is not perpendicular to its orbital plane but is tilted at an angle, and the Earth maintains this tilt consistently as it revolves around the Sun. The combination of this axial tilt and the spherical shape of the Earth gives rise to the seasons. In June, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun: sunlight strikes the Northern Hemisphere at a steeper angle and is concentrated over a smaller area, making it more intense; additionally, the Northern Hemisphere receives more than 12 hours of sunlight per day. Both effects cause higher temperatures, producing the summer season in the Northern Hemisphere. In December, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun, sunlight is spread over a larger area and is less intense, and the day is shorter than 12 hours, producing winter. The Southern Hemisphere experiences the reverse — winter in June and summer in December. A Dive Deeper box corrects two common misconceptions: that the Northern Hemisphere is warmer in summer because it is physically closer to the Sun when tilted towards it, or that seasonal temperature changes are caused by variation in Earth–Sun distance over the elliptical orbit. Both factors create distance differences that are too small to cause the observed temperature changes; in fact, the Earth is actually closest to the Sun in January. A second Dive Deeper box introduces the special dates in the yearly cycle: the summer solstice (around 21 June in the Northern Hemisphere, the longest day), the winter solstice (around 22 December, the shortest day), and the spring and autumn equinoxes (around 21 March and 23 September, when daytime lasts exactly 12 hours). A Fascinating Facts box notes that at the North Pole, the Sun rises on the equinox (21 March) and remains continuously visible for six months, setting on 22 September; the polar regions therefore experience six consecutive months of daylight followed by six months of darkness. The equator always receives 12 hours of sunlight, so the effect of seasons is minimal for regions of southern India close to the equator.

12.3 Eclipses introduces the Moon's role in creating spectacular alignment events. The Moon is a natural satellite of the Earth and revolves around the Earth as the Earth revolves around the Sun; these simultaneous orbital motions occasionally bring the Sun, Moon, and Earth into near-perfect alignment, producing eclipses.

12.3.1 Solar eclipse occurs when the Moon comes between the Sun and the Earth, obstructing the Sun's light from reaching part of the Earth. The section introduces the key concept of apparent size — the size of an object as perceived by an observer, which depends on both its actual physical size and its distance. Although the Moon is much smaller than the Sun, it is also much closer to the Earth, so their apparent sizes as seen from the Earth are nearly equal. Activity 12.4 demonstrates apparent size by asking students to cover a friend's head with an outstretched thumb — possible despite the thumb being much smaller than the head, because the thumb is much closer. When the Moon's shadow falls on a small area of the Earth's surface, observers in that area see the Sun completely blocked — a total solar eclipse — and it turns dark for a few minutes during the day. In the surrounding area where the Moon only partially blocks the Sun, observers see a partial solar eclipse. A Dive Deeper box explains why Mercury and Venus, despite being larger than the Moon, cannot block the Sun: they are so much farther from the Earth that their apparent sizes are far smaller than the Sun's, so they can only appear as tiny black dots crossing the Sun's face (a Transit of Venus). The section includes a caution that directly viewing the Sun during an eclipse — with the naked eye, sunglasses, binoculars, or a telescope — is extremely dangerous and can cause permanent blindness; the safe way to observe is to attend events organised by planetaria or astronomy clubs, or to project the Sun's image onto a screen using a mirror. A Fascinating Facts box notes that eclipses are known as grahan in Sanskrit and many Indian languages, and that ancient Indian astronomical texts — most notably the Surya Siddhanta — provided precise calculations to predict them. A Know a Scientist feature profiles M.K. Vainu Bappu, known as the father of modern Indian astronomy, who established telescopes at Nainital and Kavalur and travelled around the world to observe solar eclipses; the observatory at Kavalur is named in his honour.

12.3.2 Lunar eclipse occurs when the Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon, and the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon, blocking sunlight from reaching it. A total lunar eclipse occurs when the Moon is completely inside the Earth's shadow; the Moon does not disappear entirely but takes on a dark red colour because some sunlight is refracted through the Earth's atmosphere and reaches the Moon. A partial lunar eclipse occurs when only part of the Moon enters the Earth's shadow while the rest remains visible. Unlike solar eclipses, lunar eclipses can be safely observed with the naked eye. A Science and Society box recommends the free Stellarium computer application for finding upcoming solar and lunar eclipses visible from any location. A Fascinating Facts box describes the Kodaikanal Solar Observatory, established in 1899 in the Palani hills of southern India, which has provided over 125 years of solar observational data and is operated by the Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA), Bengaluru.

CHAPTER SUMMARY:

Chapter 1: Exploring the Investigative World of Science

Chapter 1 is an orientation chapter that introduces Grade 8 students to the investigative nature of science and previews the year's themes. It does not introduce a single scientific topic in depth but instead establishes the mindset, vocabulary, and habits of thinking that will run through all subsequent chapters.

Probe and ponder

The chapter opens with a "Probe and ponder" box addressed directly to students. It poses three curiosity questions — why is one side of a puri thinner than the other, whether there are more grains of sand on Earth's beaches and deserts or more stars in the Milky Way, and why nature has created such vast biological diversity. These questions are not meant for examination; they are framed as invitations to personal curiosity. Students are asked to write their own question in the space provided, establishing from the outset that science begins with wondering.

The investigative world of science — a Grade 8 orientation

The chapter explains that the Grade 8 book, titled Curiosity, continues a three-year progression. In Grade 6, students discovered how science begins with wonder. In Grade 7, they learnt that science is always evolving and that answers open new questions. In Grade 8, the emphasis moves to investigation: students are expected not merely to learn facts but to learn how to find new facts. The chapter distinguishes investigation from simple observation, stating that Grade 8 students can now ask more focused questions, design simple experiments, and use observations to improve understanding. The goal is for students to become investigators — young scientists exploring real-world puzzles ranging from everyday phenomena like rising dough to planetary-scale questions like global warming.

The chapter then provides a panoramic preview of the year's content, organised as a connected narrative rather than a table of contents. It traces a conceptual arc from the very small to the very large: beginning with microbes invisible to the naked eye in a drop of water, moving to human health and infection, then to electric current and its heating and magnetic effects, then to forces and pressure, then to weather phenomena including winds and cyclones, then to the particulate nature of matter and classification into elements, compounds and mixtures, then to solutions, then to light and its reflection and refraction through mirrors and lenses, then to the Moon's phases and their role in the development of calendars, and finally to ecosystems and Earth's unique capacity to support life. This previewing section demonstrates to students how the chapters are conceptually linked — forces explain pressure, pressure explains weather, particle structure explains solutions, light explains the Moon's appearance, and so on.

The chapter also draws attention to two recurring visual symbols in the textbook design: roots at the bottom of left-hand pages, symbolising groundedness in careful observation and cultural heritage, and a kite at the top of right-hand pages, symbolising the freedom of creative thinking. These are introduced not as decorative elements but as a deliberate pedagogical metaphor — good scientific investigation requires both firm grounding in evidence and imaginative inquiry.

To help you think like a scientist: Why is one side of a puri thinner than the other?

The second half of the chapter is an extended worked example of scientific investigation built around a kitchen observation. The example is introduced with the reminder that science does not require a formal laboratory — even a home kitchen provides sufficient opportunity for observation and experiment. The phenomenon chosen is the puffing of a puri, batura, or phulka when placed in hot oil or on a flame, and specifically the fact that one side of a puri is thinner than the other.

The chapter walks students through the structure of a systematic investigation. The first step is framing a scientific question: what factors might affect the way a puri puffs up when fried? The chapter distinguishes between variables that can be controlled or changed — thickness of the dough, size of the rolled circle, type of flour (atta, maida), temperature of the oil, and the angle and manner in which the dough is placed in the oil — and outcomes that can be observed or measured, such as whether the puri puffs up at all (a yes/no answer) or the time it takes to puff (measured in seconds). Students are introduced to the principle of changing only one variable at a time while keeping all other conditions constant, using the example of testing three oil temperatures while keeping dough thickness and entry angle identical.

The chapter emphasises the importance of recording all observations during an experiment, including unexpected sensory details such as whether the oil splatters, smells, or smokes. It also notes that completing one round of experiments typically generates new questions — for example, whether fresh dough puffs better than stored dough, or what happens if a hole is pricked in the puri before frying. This iterative quality, where answers breed further questions, is presented as the defining feature of scientific investigation.

The chapter concludes by pointing out that even this apparently simple everyday phenomenon — the puffing of a puri — has not been completely explained by scientists, making it an authentic and not merely pedagogical example. The closing paragraph connects the puri example to the Moon's phases, reminding students that the same habit of careful observation applies whether the subject is a kitchen experiment or a celestial phenomenon. The chapter ends with the phrase "Happy investigating!" — reinforcing the tone of curiosity and openness that the entire Grade 8 programme is designed to cultivate.

CHAPTER SUMMARY:

Chapter 2: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye

The chapter opens by explaining that the human eye cannot see objects below a certain size, and that the invention of the lens — shaped like a lentil seed — and subsequently the microscope, revealed a hidden world of tiny living creatures. Robert Hooke (1665) used a microscope to observe cork slices, naming the compartments he saw "cells." Around the same time Antonie van Leeuwenhoek built improved microscopes and became the first to clearly see and describe bacteria and blood cells, earning him the title Father of Microbiology. The chapter introduces student Activity 2.1, in which a water-filled round-bottom flask is used to demonstrate magnification before a real magnifying glass is used.

2.1 What Is a Cell?

All living beings are made up of cells. This section establishes the basic structure of a cell through Activity 2.2 (a teacher demonstration involving an onion peel stained with safranin and observed under a microscope) and Activity 2.3 (a student-executed investigation in which cheek cells are scraped, stained with methylene blue, and observed). Both activities show three fundamental components: the cell membrane (outer boundary, porous, controls entry and exit of materials), the cytoplasm (fills the interior, contains carbohydrates, proteins, fats, mineral salts, site of most life processes), and the nucleus (regulates all cellular activities and growth). Plant cells additionally have a cell wall that provides rigidity and strength, and a large vacuole that stores substances, removes waste, and maintains cell shape. A "step further" box introduces plastids (including chloroplasts that contain chlorophyll and enable photosynthesis) and mitochondria as additional plant cell components. Animal cells generally lack a cell wall and large vacuoles.

2.1.1 Variation in shape and structure of cells

Different cell types have distinct shapes that reflect their functions. Muscle cells are spindle-shaped and flexible, enabling wave-like contractions that push food through the food pipe and churn food in the stomach; other stomach cells produce digestive juices and acid. Nerve cells (neurons) are very long with branches that allow them to carry messages rapidly across the body. Cheek cells are thin and flat, forming a protective lining. Plant cells vary from rectangular to elongated to tube-like; some form tubes that carry water throughout the plant. The section establishes the principle that cell shape, size, and structure are directly related to the function the cell performs.

2.2 What Are the Levels of Organisation in the Body of a Living Organism?

This section introduces the hierarchy of biological organisation: Cell → Tissue → Organ → Organ system → Organism. A cell is the basic unit, analogous to a brick; similar cells group into tissues; tissues combine to form organs; organs cooperate in organ systems; all systems together constitute the organism. Complex organisms begin life as a single egg cell that divides repeatedly to produce many cells — such organisms are called multicellular organisms. Animals, plants, and humans are all multicellular. An "Ever heard of" box notes that the ostrich egg yolk is the largest known single cell, measuring 130–170 mm in diameter.

2.3 What Are Microorganisms?

Some living organisms are made up of just one or very few cells and are too small to see with the naked eye; these are called microorganisms or microbes. Bacteria and Amoeba are unicellular; some fungi and algae are multicellular microorganisms. Microorganisms are found in water, soil, air, and inside the body. Observing them requires a microscope that magnifies 100–400 times, though low-cost foldable paper microscopes are also referenced. Activity 2.4 involves collecting and observing pond or stagnant water under a microscope; Activity 2.5 involves observing soil suspension. Activity 2.6 presents data tables identifying organisms found in pond water (Amoeba, Paramecium — protozoa; algae) and soil suspension (bread mould and mould — fungi; algae; bacteria of spherical, comma, spiral, and rod shapes). Viruses are introduced in an "Ever heard of" box as microscopic, acellular entities that multiply only inside living cells and can infect plants, animals, and bacteria.

2.4 How Are We Connected to Microbes?

This section explores the ubiquitous presence of microorganisms — in water, soil, air, food, extreme environments such as hot springs and snow, and inside the human gut (helping with digestion, as introduced in Grade 7). The chapter uses the example of fruit or food rotting when left out to show that microbes are ever-present and can infect food. It notes that high concentrations of salt or sugar (used in pickles and murabbas) inhibit microbial growth.

2.4.1 Key players in cleaning the environment

Activity 2.7 has students layer fruit and vegetable peels with soil and observe after 2–3 weeks, finding that the peels decompose into dark, nutrient-rich manure. Bacteria and fungi in the soil break down complex plant waste into simpler substances through decomposition — returning nutrients to the soil and supporting plant growth. Microbes also decompose dead animals and animal dung. The section references the "Our scientific heritage" box noting that ancient Indian Vedic texts (particularly the Atharvaveda) reference tiny entities called 'Krimi' — both visible (Drishya) and invisible (Adrishya) — and describe their beneficial and harmful effects. A "step further" box explains that some bacteria and fungi living in oxygen-free environments decompose organic waste and release biogas (primarily methane and carbon dioxide), used as fuel for cooking, heating, electricity generation, and vehicles.

2.4.2 Microorganisms and food

Activity 2.8 compares yeast-added dough (bowl A) with plain dough (bowl B) after several hours in a warm place, showing that yeast (a fungus) breaks down sugar in warm conditions, releasing carbon dioxide that makes dough rise and become fluffy, with a small amount of alcohol responsible for altered smell. This property is used in making breads, cakes, idlis, dosas, and bhatura (the latter with Lactobacillus). Activity 2.9 tests curd formation by adding a spoonful of curd to lukewarm milk (bowl A) and cold milk (bowl B): Lactobacillus in warm bowl A ferments milk sugar (lactose), producing lactic acid that sets the curd and makes it sour; cold bowl B does not curdle. Rhizobium bacteria, living in root nodules of legumes (beans, peas, lentils), trap atmospheric nitrogen and make it available to plants, reducing the need for chemical fertilisers and explaining why farmers rotate legumes with other crops.

2.4.3 Amazing microalgae: tiny helpers in water

Microalgae are microscopic, plant-like organisms found in water, soil, air, and on trees; they produce food through photosynthesis and in doing so supply more than half of Earth's oxygen. They are nutrient-rich food sources for aquatic animals. Specific examples — Spirulina, Chlorella, and Diatoms — are used as health supplements and medicines; microalgae also help clean water and serve as biofuel feedstock. An "Ever heard of" box highlights Spirulina as a superfood rich in protein (over 60% of body weight), vitamin B12, and low in fat and sugar, and describes how it can be cultivated in a glass tank. The section warns that pollution, climate change, and habitat destruction threaten microalgal diversity and that their conservation is important for environmental protection and oxygen balance.

2.5 Why Is Cell Considered to Be a Basic Unit of Life?

This concluding section consolidates the chapter's core argument: all living organisms — plants, animals, and microorganisms — are built from cells. Multicellular organisms have specialised cells that cooperate; unicellular organisms (bacteria, protozoa) carry out all life functions in a single cell. Fungi can be either (yeast = unicellular; mould = multicellular). The cells of microorganisms share a cell membrane with plant and animal cells; fungal cells additionally have a cell wall but lack chloroplasts; bacteria lack a well-defined nucleus and nuclear membrane, possessing instead a nucleoid region — this is the key structural distinction between bacteria and all other cell types. The section notes that an electron microscope (magnification ~10,00,000 times) is needed to observe sub-cellular components that will be studied in higher classes.

content.text:
CHAPTER SUMMARY:

Chapter 3: Health: The Ultimate Treasure

3.1 Health: Is It More Than Not Falling Sick?

This section challenges the assumption that health means simply not having a disease, broadening the concept to include physical, mental, and social dimensions. The World Health Organization defines health as "a state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being, and not merely the absence of disease." A healthy person performs tasks efficiently, copes well with difficult situations, and adjusts successfully with peers and society. The section also introduces the Ayurvedic perspective — that true health involves a balance of body, mind, and surroundings, supported by dinacharya, ritucharya, and practices like yoga and meditation. Activity 3.1 presents a student case study in which social isolation and excessive screen time lead to physical and mental symptoms, prompting reflection on how habits and surroundings affect well-being.

3.2 How Can We Stay Healthy?

This section frames good health as the outcome of both lifestyle choices and environmental conditions. Nutritious food, personal hygiene, clean surroundings, regular exercise, adequate sleep, positive relationships, and a positive attitude all contribute to staying healthy. Activity 3.2 asks students to list good and harmful habits, then discuss findings with peers to recognise that health is shaped by lifestyle and environment.

3.2.1 Maintain a healthy lifestyle

This subsection lists specific lifestyle practices that support health: eating a balanced diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and whole grains; avoiding processed, fatty, and sugary food; staying physically active through outdoor play, walking, or cycling; limiting screen time; getting enough sleep; practising yoga or pranayama regularly; and refusing harmful substances such as tobacco, alcohol, and addictive drugs. The key terms introduced are lifestyle and the specific categories of healthy and harmful habits.

3.2.2 Keep the environment clean

This subsection establishes that a clean environment is as essential to health as personal habits. Activity 3.3 has students compare two playground images — one clean and one polluted — to understand why people in polluted surroundings fall sick more often. It introduces the Air Quality Index (AQI) as a monitoring tool and notes that vehicle and factory pollution can cause asthma and respiratory problems. The section also notes that even a clean environment cannot compensate for poor emotional or social well-being — relationships and feelings matter equally.

3.3 How Do We Know That We Are Unwell?

This section introduces the distinction between symptoms and signs of illness. A symptom is defined as what a person feels subjectively, such as pain, tiredness, or dizziness. A sign is something that can be observed or measured by others, such as fever, rash, high blood pressure, or swelling. The section frames these two categories as the tools that help doctors understand the cause of illness and notes that the body's deviation from its normal functioning is what constitutes being unwell.

3.4 Diseases: What Are the Causes and Types?

This section introduces the concept of disease as a condition that disrupts the normal functioning of the body or mind, often affecting one or more organ systems. The key term pathogen is introduced to describe disease-causing organisms including bacteria, viruses, fungi, worms, and protozoa. The chapter establishes a fundamental classification of diseases into two major types: communicable diseases, which are caused by pathogens and can spread from person to person, and non-communicable diseases (NCDs), which are linked to lifestyle, diet, or environment and do not spread between people. Examples given for communicable diseases include typhoid, dengue, flu, chickenpox, and COVID-19. Examples of NCDs include cancer, diabetes, and asthma. The section notes that NCDs have become the leading cause of death in India due to changes in lifestyle such as consumption of processed food, reduced physical activity, and an aging population.

3.4.1 How are communicable diseases caused and spread?

This subsection examines how pathogens spread, identifying five routes: airborne transmission (coughs or sneezes), direct contact (handshaking), indirect contact (shared personal items), contaminated food or water, and vectors (insects such as mosquitoes and houseflies). Activity 3.4 presents Table 3.1, a student-completed table grouping common communicable diseases by transmission mode — airborne diseases (common cold, influenza, chickenpox, measles, tuberculosis), waterborne and foodborne diseases (hepatitis A, cholera, typhoid, ascariasis), and insect-transmitted diseases (malaria, dengue). For each disease the table records the causal agent, site of infection, symptoms, and preventive measures. The subsection also introduces parasites — organisms such as intestinal worms that live in or on a host and feed on its nutrients. Key preventive practices include handwashing, covering the mouth while coughing, wearing masks, avoiding shared personal items, and maintaining food and water hygiene.

3.4.2 How are non-communicable diseases caused?

This subsection explains that NCDs such as cancer, diabetes, and asthma arise from lifestyle, diet, and environmental factors rather than pathogens. Deficiency diseases — such as scurvy, anaemia, and goitre — are also classified as NCDs caused by nutrient deficiencies. Chronic diseases are defined as conditions persisting for more than three months. Diabetes is highlighted as a major NCD in India, driven by hormonal imbalances, unhealthy diet, physical inactivity, and obesity. Activity 3.5 asks students to survey their neighbourhood for common lifestyle-related diseases and fill in a table of disease names, symptoms, and suggested lifestyle changes.

3.5 How to Prevent and Control Diseases?

This section establishes the principle that prevention is preferable to cure for both communicable and non-communicable diseases. Activity 3.6 presents a case study from Bhadrak district, Odisha, where a community sanitation campaign improved toilet use, reduced open defecation, and led to fewer cases of diarrhoea and infections in children, illustrating the power of simple sanitation steps.

Ability of the body to fight diseases

This subsection introduces immunity — the body's natural ability to resist disease — and the immune system that provides it. Vaccines train the immune system by exposing it to weakened, dead, or harmless parts of a pathogen, producing acquired immunity. The historical example of Edward Jenner's smallpox vaccine is developed through a "Think like a scientist" framework: his observation that cowpox-infected milkmaids did not contract smallpox, his hypothesis, his inoculation experiment, and the eventual global eradication of smallpox by 1979. India's traditional practice of variolation by teekedaars is noted as a heritage precursor to vaccination, and India's current role as a major global vaccine producer is highlighted. Vaccines are characterised as preventive, not curative.

3.5.1 Treatment of diseases

This subsection explains that when the immune system fails, antibiotics — medicines that kill bacteria by targeting bacterial cell structures absent in human cells — may be used. They are ineffective against viruses or protozoa. The discovery of penicillin by Alexander Fleming in 1928 is presented as a "Think like a scientist" example. The subsection then addresses antibiotic resistance, where bacteria survive and multiply despite antibiotic treatment due to overuse or incomplete dosing. Activity 3.7 asks students to infer from an infographic how resistance develops and what precautions reduce it. Traditional medicine systems such as Ayurveda, Siddha, and Unani use natural substances like herbs and oils and can support everyday well-being, but may not be effective for all diseases or stages. For NCDs, treatment focuses on managing symptoms through medication, lifestyle changes, and rehabilitation, with early diagnosis and continuous care being key.

CHAPTER SUMMARY:

Chapter 4: Electricity: Magnetic and Heating Effects

Section 4.1 opens with a contextual story of students observing a lifting electromagnet at a science exhibition — an iron nail wrapped with wire and connected to a battery picks up iron clips when the circuit is closed, and releases them when the circuit is opened. This motivates the central question of whether electric current has a magnetic effect.

4.1 Does an Electric Current Have a Magnetic Effect?

This section investigates the magnetic effect of electric current through a student activity (Activity 4.1) in which a magnetic compass is placed under a current-carrying wire. Students observe that when the switch is closed and current flows, the compass needle deflects; when the switch is opened, the needle returns to its original position. The section introduces the term magnetic field as the region around a magnet or current-carrying wire where magnetic effects can be detected. The key concept established is the magnetic effect of electric current: a current-carrying conductor produces a magnetic field around it, which disappears when the current stops. The section contains a "Be a scientist" sidebar about Hans Christian Oersted (1777–1851), who first discovered the link between electricity and magnetism in 1820. The section also notes that this magnetic effect has practical applications in devices such as electromagnets, electric bells, motors, fans, and loudspeakers. There is a student activity present.

4.1.1 Electromagnets

This subsection builds on the magnetic effect to introduce electromagnets. Activity 4.2 ("Let us explore") has students wrap an insulated wire around an iron nail, connect it to a cell, and test whether the nail attracts iron paper clips; clips cling when current flows and fall off when current is stopped. Activity 4.3 ("Let us experiment") extends this by forming a cylindrical coil on a paper cylinder, placing magnetic compasses at both ends, and inserting an iron nail into the core. Students observe that the coil with current behaves like a magnet and that inserting the iron nail increases the magnetic strength significantly. The section defines an electromagnet as a current-carrying coil that behaves as a magnet, noting that practical electromagnets have an iron core for greater strength. Activity 4.4 ("Let us investigate") has students identify the poles of the electromagnet using a compass, establishing that an electromagnet has a North pole and a South pole, just like a bar magnet. A "Think like a scientist" box guides students to vary the number of cells and the number of turns to discover that electromagnet strength depends on the magnitude of current and the number of coil turns, and that its poles can be reversed by reversing current direction. A "A step further" sidebar explains Earth's magnetic field as arising from movement of liquid iron in Earth's core, linking the chapter's physics to a real-world natural phenomenon. There are multiple student activities and one teacher-guided investigation present.

4.1.2 Lifting Electromagnets

This short subsection connects the electromagnet concept to an industrial application. It describes lifting electromagnets mounted on cranes that are used in factories and scrap yards to move, lift, and sort heavy metal objects. The crane operator controls the magnet by switching the current on and off — when current is on, the electromagnet holds objects; when current is off, the magnetic field disappears and objects are released. A "step further" sidebar notes that in higher grades students will learn about electromagnetic induction — that just as electricity produces magnetism, a moving magnet can produce an electric current. There is no student activity in this subsection.

4.2 Does a Current Carrying Wire Get Hot?

This section introduces the heating effect of electric current. Activity 4.5 ("Let us observe") uses a nichrome wire connected in a circuit: students touch the wire before and after current flows to observe that it becomes warm when current passes through it. The section explains the mechanism: when current flows through a conductor, the conductor offers resistance to the flow, and this resistance converts some electrical energy into heat energy. The term heating effect of electric current is introduced to describe this phenomenon. A "Think like a scientist" box has students compare heating with one cell versus two cells, leading to the conclusion that the amount of heat generated depends on the magnitude of electric current, as well as the material, thickness, length of the wire, and duration of current flow. The section connects to everyday appliances — electric room heaters, stoves, kettles, irons, immersion rods, and hair dryers — all of which use a heating element (a rod or coil of wire). The section also notes the dual nature of the heating effect: it is useful in appliances but can cause problems such as energy loss during transmission, overheating, melting of plastic parts, or fires. Industrial applications such as electric furnaces for melting scrap steel are mentioned in a sidebar. There is a student activity present.

4.3 How Does a Battery Generate Electricity?

This section shifts focus from the effects of electric current to the source of electric current in portable form. It opens the question of what is inside cells and batteries that produces electricity.

4.3.1 Voltaic Cell

This subsection describes the Voltaic cell (also called Galvanic cell), one of the earliest electric cells. It consists of two metal electrodes (rods of different materials) partially immersed in a liquid electrolyte — typically a weak acid or salt solution — held in a glass or plastic container. A chemical reaction between the electrodes and the electrolyte produces electricity. When the circuit is connected, current flows from the positive terminal through the circuit to the negative terminal. Over time the chemicals are consumed and the cell becomes "dead." An "Ever heard of" sidebar narrates the historical discovery by Alessandro Volta and Luigi Galvani in the late 1700s, including Galvani's observation that a dead frog's leg twitched when touched with two different metals and Volta's counter-experiment using saltwater-soaked paper to prove it was the metal-liquid combination — not the frog — that generated current. Activity 4.6 ("Let us construct") has students build a Voltaic cell using lemons, copper wires, and iron nails to power a LED, reinforcing the concept that lemon juice acts as the electrolyte. There is a student activity present.

4.3.2 Dry Cells

This subsection describes the dry cell as the most widely used type of electric cell today. Unlike the Voltaic cell, the electrolyte in a dry cell is not a liquid but a thick moist paste, making it more portable and practical. The structure consists of a zinc container (negative terminal), a central carbon rod with a metal cap (positive terminal), and the paste-like electrolyte surrounding the carbon rod. The dry cell is a single-use cell — once the chemicals are used up it must be disposed of. The subsection notes that rechargeable batteries are increasingly replacing single-use cells for many applications. There is no student activity in this subsection.

4.3.3 Rechargeable Batteries

This subsection introduces rechargeable batteries, which can be recharged and reused multiple times, preventing waste and reducing cost over time. Different types are mentioned — from small batteries in watches and phones to larger ones in laptops, inverters, and electric vehicles. The section notes that even rechargeable batteries wear out after many charge-discharge cycles. A "step further" sidebar focuses on lithium-ion (Li-ion) batteries as the most common type today, mentions resource scarcity concerns around lithium and cobalt, and introduces solid-state batteries as a future technology promising greater safety and longer life. A safety sidebar notes that "dead" batteries are not completely harmless and should be disposed of at e-waste recycling facilities, as they may contain acids and toxic metals. There is no student activity in this subsection.

CHAPTER SUMMARY:

Chapter 5: Exploring Forces

Section 5.1 — What Is a Force? introduces the concept of force through a simple student activity. Activity 5.1 asks students to move a large cardboard box in as many ways as they can, leading them to discover that every mode of movement — pushing, pulling, lifting, carrying — involves a push or pull. The section establishes the foundational definition: a push or pull applied on an object is called force in science.

Section 5.2 — What Can a Force Do to the Objects on Which It Is Applied? uses Activity 5.2, a structured analytical exercise in which students examine everyday force situations (a friend pulling a moving bicycle to stop it, hitting a ball with a bat, pressing an inflated balloon) and record what effect the force has in each case. Through this analysis, the section identifies the four possible effects of force: making an object at rest begin to move, changing the speed of a moving object, changing the direction of motion of an object, and bringing about a change in the shape of an object.

Section 5.3 — Are Forces an Interaction Between Two or More Objects? establishes the interactional nature of force. The section asks students to count how many objects are involved in each force situation from Section 5.2, guiding them to infer that at least two objects must interact for a force to come into play. It formally defines force as a push or pull on an object resulting from that object's interaction with another object, and introduces the SI unit of force: newton (N), symbolised as N. A Step Further extension notes that when two objects interact each experiences a force from the other, and that these forces disappear the moment interaction ceases.

Section 5.4 — What Are the Different Types of Forces? organises forces into two broad categories: contact forces and non-contact forces.

Section 5.4.1 — Contact forces are those that require physical contact — direct (hand, body parts) or indirect (stick, rope) — between the objects involved. Muscular force is the first contact force introduced: it is the force produced by the contraction and elongation of muscles during any physical activity (walking, running, lifting, pushing). Animals, birds, fish, and insects also rely on muscular force for movement and survival; humans historically harnessed animal muscular force for tasks like ploughing and transport. A sidebar notes that muscular force also drives internal body functions such as digestion and circulation of blood through the heart. The second contact force is friction. Introduced through observations of objects slowing and stopping on their own, the section poses the question of what hidden force causes this. Activity 5.3 asks students to push an object across a surface and observe that it stops, while Activity 5.4 repeats the push on different surfaces (glass, cloth, wood, ceramic tile, sand) and observes that the stopping distance differs. These activities establish that friction is the contact force that acts between two surfaces in contact and always opposes the direction of motion. The mechanism of friction is explained: even apparently smooth surfaces have minute irregularities that interlock with each other. A Step Further note extends friction to objects moving through liquids and gases (air drag on aeroplanes, ships) and explains streamlining.

Section 5.4.2 — Non-contact forces are those that act at a distance without physical contact. Magnetic force is introduced first: students already know from Grade 6 that magnets attract magnetic materials and that like poles repel while unlike poles attract. Activity 5.5 asks students to stack two ring magnets on a vertical stick with like poles facing each other, observe that the upper magnet floats, and feel the repulsive force when pushed down. The formal definition establishes that magnetic force is a non-contact force exerted by a magnet on another magnet or a magnetic material. Electrostatic force follows: Activity 5.6 has students rub a plastic scale or straw with polythene and bring it near small paper pieces without touching them — the paper is attracted. Activity 5.7 has students rub two balloons with a woollen cloth, observe that the two identically charged balloons repel each other, and then bring the woollen cloth near one balloon, observing attraction. The section explains that rubbing causes static charges to build up; similar charges repel and unlike charges attract. The formal definition is that electrostatic force is the force exerted by a charged body on another charged or uncharged body; it is a non-contact force. A Step Further connects moving charges to electric current. Gravitational force is the final non-contact force. Activity 5.8 prompts students to throw a ball upwards and observe that it always returns to the ground regardless of how hard it is thrown. The section defines gravitational force as the force with which the Earth attracts objects towards itself, also called force of gravity or gravity. Unlike magnetic and electrostatic force, gravitational force is always attractive, never repulsive. The section describes the vertical motion of objects under gravity — rising objects slow down, stop momentarily, reverse direction, and accelerate downward.

Section 5.5 — Weight and Its Measurement distinguishes weight from mass. Weight is defined as the force with which the Earth pulls an object towards itself; it is measured in newtons. Activity 5.9 has students hang different objects (pencil box, tiffin box, small stone) from a spring one by one and observe that different objects stretch the spring by different amounts, demonstrating that the Earth pulls different objects with different forces. A Step Further box describes a spring balance — its hook, spring, and graduated scale in N — and explains how to read it. Activities 5.10 and 5.11 guide students to identify the range and the least count of a spring balance, and Activity 5.12 uses the spring balance to measure the weight of different objects. The section then distinguishes mass (the amount of matter in an object, measured in kg, constant everywhere) from weight (the gravitational force on an object, which varies with location and can be very different on other planets). A Step Further table shows that the same 1 kg object weighs 10 N on Earth, 1.6 N on the Moon, 3.8 N on Mars, 9 N on Venus, and 25.4 N on Jupiter.

Section 5.6 — Floating and Sinking addresses the upward force exerted by liquids on submerged objects. Activity 5.13 has students push a sealed empty bottle into a bucket of water, feel the upward push, release the bottle, and observe it bounce back to the surface. This leads to the definition of upthrust or buoyant force as the force applied by a liquid on an object in the upward direction. The section explains that when an object is placed in a liquid, gravitational force acts downward on it while buoyant force acts upward; if gravitational force exceeds buoyant force the object sinks, if they are equal the object floats. The density of the liquid is mentioned as one factor that determines buoyant force. A Step Further introduces Archimedes' Principle: the upward force on an immersed object equals the weight of the liquid it displaces. A sidebar notes that pumice, a volcanic rock full of air pockets, floats on water because its density is less than that of water.

content.text:
CHAPTER SUMMARY:

Chapter 6: Pressure, Winds, Storms, and Cyclones

6.1 Pressure

This section introduces the concept of pressure as force per unit area, motivated by a relatable scenario of two children carrying bags with narrow and broad straps. The key term introduced is pressure, defined as Pressure = Force / Area. The section establishes that when the same force is distributed over a smaller area, the resulting pressure is higher — which is why narrow-strap bags feel more uncomfortable than broad-strap bags. The SI unit of pressure is newton per metre squared (N/m²), also called pascal (Pa). The section includes a student activity (Table 6.1) in which students compare driving an iron nail by its head versus its pointed end, and cutting an apple with the sharp versus the blunt edge of a knife, to observe how area affects pressure.

The section then extends pressure to liquids, using the example of overhead water tanks placed at a height to supply good water pressure. Activity 6.1 involves two pipes of different diameters with balloons attached; when filled to the same water level, both balloons bulge equally, demonstrating that liquid pressure depends on the height of the water column, not on the volume or weight of water above. Activity 6.2 involves holes made near the bottom of a plastic bottle — when unsealed, water sprays outward in all directions, showing that liquids exert pressure not only at the bottom of a container but also on its sides and in all directions. A sidebar ("Ever heard of…") explains why dam bases are broader than their tops — to withstand the large horizontal water pressure near the bottom.

6.2 Pressure Exerted by Air

This section establishes that the atmosphere exerts pressure on all objects. Activity 6.3 involves an inverted paper plate covered first with a folded and then an unfolded chart paper sheet, lifted by a stick — more effort is needed with the unfolded (larger-area) sheet, demonstrating that air exerts a force that increases with area, which is the definition of atmospheric pressure. The section introduces the term atmospheric pressure — the pressure exerted by the air around us. Activity 6.4 uses a rubber sucker pressed on a smooth surface; it sticks because pressing pushes out the air inside, making the surrounding atmospheric pressure higher than the pressure inside the sucker, so it becomes difficult to pull off. The section quantifies atmospheric pressure by noting that the force exerted by the air column over an area of 15 cm × 15 cm is nearly equal to the weight of a 225 kg object (2250 N). It explains that humans are not crushed because the pressure inside the body equals the atmospheric pressure. A "step further" box notes that practical units for air pressure are millibar (mb) and hectopascal (hPa), both equal to 100 Pa.

6.3 Formation of Wind

This section establishes that winds form because air moves from regions of high pressure to regions of low pressure. Activity 6.5 connects an inflated balloon to an uninflated one via a straw; air moves from the inflated (higher pressure) balloon to the uninflated (lower pressure) one, and the flow stops when pressures equalise — demonstrating the directional movement of air driven by pressure differences. The section then connects this principle to sea breeze and land breeze: during the day, land heats faster than the sea, air above land rises and creates a low-pressure area, and cooler sea air flows in (sea breeze); at night, the sea is warmer, so the reverse occurs (land breeze). It also notes that a larger pressure difference produces higher wind speeds.

6.4 High-Speed Winds Result in Lowering of Air Pressure

This section introduces the inverse relationship between wind speed and air pressure. Activity 6.6 involves blowing air between two inflated balloons hanging from a stick; the balloons move towards each other, because the high-speed air between them creates a low-pressure zone while surrounding higher-pressure air pushes them inward — and blowing harder accelerates this effect. The section applies this principle to explain why roofs of houses may be blown off during storms: high-speed winds over a roof create low pressure above it, while pressure inside the house remains higher, generating an upward net force. The safety recommendation given is to keep doors and windows open during storms so wind can pass through the house, reducing this pressure difference and protecting the roof.

6.5 Storms, Thunderstorms, and Lightning

This section explains how storms, thunderstorms, and lightning form through a chain of atmospheric processes. When land is heated, warm moist air rises to form a low-pressure area; cooler surrounding air rushes in, gets heated, and rises in turn, creating a continuous wind circulation. As rising air expands and cools, water vapour condenses to form clouds; when droplets merge into heavy drops, they fall as rain, hail, or snow — and the resulting strong winds accompanying rain constitute a storm. Under certain conditions, rising warm air reaches heights cold enough to convert water droplets into ice particles. Strong upward and downward winds cause water droplets and ice particles to rub against each other, generating static electric charges within clouds — lighter positively charged ice particles rise to the upper cloud layers while heavier negatively charged water droplets occupy the lower layers. This charge separation eventually causes the ground beneath to become positively charged. When the charge build-up is large enough to break down air's insulating property, a sudden discharge — lightning — occurs within clouds, between clouds, or between clouds and the ground. The rapid heating and expansion of air by lightning produces the sound of thunder, and a storm with both lightning and thunder is called a thunderstorm. A "step further" box notes regional names for pre-monsoon thunderstorms in India (Kalboishakhi, Bordoisila, mango showers). The section closes with safety precautions during lightning: crouch low in open areas, avoid tall objects and metallic umbrellas, leave water bodies, and stay inside vehicles. A sidebar describes lightning conductors — metallic rods installed on buildings with a pointed end above the highest point and the other end buried in the ground — which provide a safe discharge path for electrical charges.

6.6 Cyclone

This section explains the formation, structure, and effects of cyclones. Cyclones form over warm ocean water: heating causes warm moist air to rise, water vapour condenses and releases latent heat back into the atmosphere, further warming the ascending air and deepening the low-pressure centre. Air from surrounding high-pressure regions rushes in, Earth's rotation causes the incoming air to spin, and the self-reinforcing cycle builds a very low-pressure area with high-speed revolving winds — forming a cyclone. The calm, lowest-pressure centre of a cyclone is called the eye of the cyclone; the surrounding region experiences intense winds and heavy rainfall. A cyclone intensifies over the ocean but weakens once it reaches land, as the source of moist air is cut off. The section describes the destructive effects of cyclones: storm surges of 3–12 metres flooding coastal areas, river flooding and landslides from heavy rainfall, contamination of drinking water by seawater, reduced soil fertility from salt deposition, blocked roads, and extended power outages. The section emphasises cyclone preparedness — monitoring IMD alerts and weather satellites, keeping emergency kits, and moving to designated cyclone shelters. The example of Cyclone Amphan (2020) with peak winds of 270 km/h is cited to illustrate the scale of cyclone destruction.

ARUVI — CLOSING SYNTHESIS RE-AUTHORING · SCIENCE · MIDDLE STAGE

You are re-writing ONE unit: the closing whole-chapter synthesis of a chapter's fullest
lesson plan. This unit is served in two situations, and it must be excellent in both:

1. As the FINAL unit of the fullest plan — the class finishes the chapter with it.
2. As ONE EXTRA 45-minute period appended to a SHORTER complete plan of the same

THE UNIT YOU ARE WRITING closes the chapter through one fresh, concrete application: a
scenario, artefact, dataset, place or design problem the chapter itself never uses. The
class brings the chapter's concepts; the unit puts them to work in the new setting, and
what the task shows IS the synthesis — the chapter drawn together by using it whole, not
by summarising it.

content.text:
CHAPTER SUMMARY:

Chapter 7: Particulate Nature of Matter

Section 7.1 introduces the central question of what matter is made up of. Through Activity 7.1 (breaking and grinding chalk), students explore whether matter can be subdivided indefinitely. The activity establishes that even after grinding chalk to fine powder, each speck remains chalk — a physical change only. The key term introduced is constituent particle: the basic indivisible unit that makes up a larger piece of a substance. Activity 7.2 (dissolving sugar in water) reinforces this idea. After stirring, sugar particles become invisible yet their presence is confirmed by taste; the chapter explains that sugar breaks into its constituent particles, which occupy the interparticle spaces between water molecules. These two activities together establish the foundational idea that all matter is composed of an extremely large number of very small particles invisible even under an ordinary microscope.

Section 7.2 addresses what determines the physical state of matter. The chapter explains that constituent particles are held together by interparticle attractions — forces that are attractive in nature. The strength of these attractions depends on the nature of the substance and the interparticle distance, with even a slight increase in distance causing a drastic weakening of the force. A sidebar, "Our Scientific Heritage," notes that Acharya Kanad, the ancient Indian philosopher, first proposed the concept of Parmanu (atom) — tiny, indivisible, eternal particles — in his work Vaisheshika Sutras.

Subsection 7.2.1 covers the solid state. Activity 7.3 (collecting and hammering solid objects — iron nail, rock salt, stone, wood, key, aluminium) leads to the observation that all have a definite shape and volume. This is because particles in solids are tightly packed with very strong interparticle attractions that hold them in fixed positions; particles can only vibrate about their positions and cannot move past each other. When heated, vibrations intensify until the particles abandon their fixed positions and the interparticle forces weaken — this is the melting point, defined as the minimum temperature at which a solid becomes a liquid at atmospheric pressure. A data table gives melting points of ice (0°C), urea (133°C), and iron (1538°C) to illustrate how the strength of interparticle forces varies across substances.

Subsection 7.2.2 examines the liquid state. Activity 7.4 (transferring 200 mL of water across three differently shaped containers A, B, C) demonstrates that liquids take the shape of their container but maintain a fixed volume. Liquids' particles are free to move but only within a limited space, making interparticle attractions slightly weaker than in solids. The section defines boiling point as the temperature at which a liquid converts to vapour at atmospheric pressure; at this point, particles have enough energy to escape the liquid entirely, and bubble formation occurs throughout the bulk. Evaporation — which occurs at all temperatures at the surface — is distinguished as a slower process occurring even below the boiling point.

Subsection 7.2.3 explores the gaseous state. Activity 7.5 (collecting smoke from a burning incense stick in Gas Jar A, then allowing it to spread into an inverted Gas Jar B) shows that gas fills all available space. This demonstrates that gas particles move freely in all directions, interparticle attractions are negligible, and gases have neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume. An alternative demonstration using iodine vapour (solid iodine subliming inside a closed jar) is mentioned. The section concludes by classifying both liquids and gases as fluids because both flow and do not retain a fixed shape.

Section 7.3 investigates how interparticle spacing differs across the three states. Activity 7.6 (syringe experiment: compressing air by pushing a plunger, then repeating with water) establishes that gases are highly compressible because their particles have large spaces between them, while water is practically incompressible. Activity 7.7 (adding sugar to water, marking the water level before and after dissolution) shows that the solution volume is less than the sum of the individual volumes, proving that interparticle spaces exist in liquids and that dissolved particles fit into those spaces. Repeating with insoluble sand confirms the contrast: sand particles settle and add volume rather than dissolving. A summary diagram (Fig. 7.12) illustrates particle packing in the three states: minimum spacing in solids, moderate spacing in liquids, and maximum spacing in gases. A "A Step Further" sidebar clarifies that the term "particle" in Suspended Particulate Matter (SPM, referring to dust in air pollution) is different in scale from constituent particles like atoms and molecules.

Section 7.4 examines how particles move in different states. Activity 7.8 (dropping potassium permanganate into water) shows the spread of pink colour from the grain eventually reaching the entire tumbler, demonstrating that liquid particles are in constant motion. A "Think Like a Scientist" box extends this: repeating the activity with hot, room-temperature, and ice-cold water shows that particle movement — and therefore rate of spreading — increases with temperature. Activity 7.9 (burning an incense stick in one corner of a room) demonstrates that fragrance spreads throughout the space, providing evidence that gas particles are in constant, rapid, random motion that carries scent particles in all directions. The chapter closes with a synthesis paragraph explaining that thermal energy is the underlying driver: low thermal energy in solids means strong interparticle attraction and only vibration; at the melting point thermal energy overcomes attractions allowing liquid-state movement; in the gaseous state thermal energy is sufficient to overcome attractions entirely, enabling free movement. A summary table compares interparticle spacing, packing, attraction strength, and particle movement across solid, liquid, and gas states.

CHAPTER SUMMARY:

Chapter 8: Nature of Matter: Elements, Compounds, and Mixtures

This chapter explores how all matter around us is composed of substances that can be classified as mixtures, pure substances (elements or compounds), and minerals. Beginning from familiar everyday objects, the chapter builds a hierarchical understanding of the classification of matter.

8.1 What Are Mixtures?
This section introduces the concept of a mixture using familiar examples such as poha, sprout salad, sugar dissolved in water, soups, and lemonade. A mixture is defined as a combination of two or more substances where each substance retains its own properties and the components do not react chemically with each other. The individual substances in a mixture are called its components. The section distinguishes between two types of mixtures: non-uniform mixtures, where different components are visible to the naked eye or with a magnifying device (e.g., sprout salad), and uniform mixtures, where components are evenly distributed and cannot be distinguished even under a microscope (e.g., sugar dissolved in water). A sidebar introduces alloys (stainless steel, brass, bronze) as examples of uniform solid-solid mixtures, and a cultural heritage note mentions the ancient Indian concept of Mishraloha, referring to alloys described in texts like the Charaka Samhita and used for medicinal purposes.

8.1.1 Is air a mixture?
This subsection revisits the composition of air, confirmed from earlier learning, as a uniform mixture of nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide, and water vapour. It contains a student activity (Activity 8.1) in which students prepare lime water from calcium oxide and water, then expose it to air in a petri dish to observe it turning milky — demonstrating the presence of carbon dioxide through the reaction of calcium hydroxide with carbon dioxide to form calcium carbonate. A second activity (Activity 8.2) involves placing a black sheet of paper near an open window to collect and examine airborne dust particles with a magnifying glass, showing that dust is suspended in air as a pollutant. A sidebar notes major air pollutants including particulate matter and gases like carbon monoxide, ozone, nitrogen dioxide, and sulfur dioxide, and introduces the Air Quality Index (AQI).

8.1.2 Types of mixtures
This subsection extends the classification of mixtures based on the physical states of their components. A table (Table 8.1) lists six mixture types — gas-gas (e.g., air), gas-liquid (e.g., aerated water, oxygen in water), solid-gas (e.g., carbon particles in air), liquid-liquid (e.g., vinegar, oil and water), solid-liquid (e.g., sand in water, seawater), and solid-solid (e.g., baking powder, alloys) — and asks students to classify each as uniform or non-uniform. The section also clarifies that in science, all components of a mixture must be pure substances, and that the purpose of separating a mixture in science is to obtain pure substances.

8.2 What Are Pure Substances?
This section distinguishes between the common usage of the word "pure" (meaning unadulterated) and its scientific meaning. In science, a pure substance is one that contains only one kind of particle and cannot be separated into other kinds of matter by any physical process. The section notes that everyday "pure" products like milk, ghee, or spices may still be scientifically impure if they contain more than one substance. A sidebar prompts students to classify milk, packed fruit juice, baking soda, sugar, and soil as mixtures or pure substances.

8.3 What Are the Types of Pure Substances?
This section introduces the two categories of pure substances — elements and compounds — through a demonstration activity (Activity 8.3) in which electricity is passed through water (with dilute sulfuric acid added) using a 9V battery and two inverted test tubes. Unequal volumes of gas collect in the two test tubes; testing with a burning candle confirms one is hydrogen (pop sound) and the other is oxygen (flame glows brighter). The activity shows that water decomposes into two distinct gases, establishing that water is composed of two different substances.

8.3.1 Elements
The two gases produced — hydrogen and oxygen — are identified as elements, defined as pure substances made of identical particles called atoms that cannot be broken down further into simpler substances. Elements are described as the building blocks of all matter, with examples including gold, silver, sulfur, and carbon. The section notes that atoms of most elements exist as molecules: two hydrogen atoms form a molecule of hydrogen; two oxygen atoms form a molecule of oxygen. A sidebar classifies elements as metals and non-metals, mentions metalloids (like silicon and boron), and provides facts about the 118 known elements — including that eleven are gaseous at room temperature, two are liquid (mercury and bromine), and most are solid.

8.3.2 Compounds
This section explains why water cannot be separated into hydrogen and oxygen by physical means: because the particles of hydrogen and oxygen are chemically bonded in a fixed 2:1 ratio, making water a compound. Compounds are defined as substances formed when different elements combine chemically in fixed ratios, having properties entirely different from the constituent elements. Activity 8.4 (student activity) involves heating sugar in a boiling tube, which turns brown and then chars to leave carbon behind, with water droplets forming at the open end — demonstrating that sugar is a compound of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen. Activity 8.5 (demonstration activity) compares a mixture of iron filings and sulfur (Sample A) with iron sulfide produced by heating that mixture (Sample B). Students test both samples for colour, texture, magnetic attraction, and response to dilute hydrochloric acid: Sample A (mixture) retains the individual properties of iron and sulfur — iron is attracted to a magnet and reacts with HCl to produce hydrogen gas (colourless, no odour, burns with pop sound); Sample B (compound, iron sulfide) is uniformly black, not attracted to a magnet, and reacts with HCl to produce hydrogen sulfide gas (colourless, rotten egg odour). This contrast establishes the key distinction between mixtures and compounds.

8.4 How Do We Use Elements, Compounds, and Mixtures?
This section contextualises the practical importance of elements, compounds, and mixtures across everyday life and technology. Air is cited as a mixture of oxygen, nitrogen, and carbon dioxide; water as a compound of hydrogen and oxygen. Elements like iron and aluminium are used in construction and vehicles. Chemists combine elements into compounds to create medicines, vaccines, and fertilisers. Engineers and material scientists use knowledge of compounds and mixtures to develop advanced materials such as alloys (e.g., stainless steel stronger than pure iron) and building materials (wood, steel, concrete — all mixtures). A sidebar highlights graphene aerogel, a carbon-based material considered the lightest material on earth, with potential for oil-spill cleanup and energy-saving devices. A heritage note describes Dhokra art from Bihar and Odisha, where brass or bronze (alloys of elements) are cast using the lost-wax method to create traditional figures.

8.5 What Are Minerals?
This section introduces minerals as natural solid substances with a fixed chemical composition, found in rocks. Most rocks are mixtures of minerals. Some minerals called native minerals are pure elements (metals like gold, silver, copper, or non-metals like sulfur and carbon). Most minerals are compounds — examples include quartz, calcite, mica, pyroxene, and olivine. The section connects minerals to everyday materials: cement is made from calcite, quartz, alumina, and iron oxide; talcum powder comes from the mineral talc. The chapter closes by reinforcing that elements and compounds are the building blocks of matter, and that not everything (e.g., light, heat, electricity, thoughts) constitutes matter.
